lessons.title: Practical Work — Descriptive Form and Set-Builder Form
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

A set is a collection of well-defined objects. The objects in a set are called its members or elements. In this work you learn to look at the members in curly brackets { } and say in words what the set is. That is the descriptive form. You also learn the short set-builder form, which uses a rule with x.

Formula / Rule

Descriptive form = the set described in words, e.g. D = the set of the first four multiples of 3.

Set-builder form = {x / x ∈ N} reads as: the set of all x such that x belongs to N.

Symbols: N = natural numbers, W = whole numbers, Z = integers, E = even numbers, O = odd numbers.

Worked Example

Example: Write D = {3, 6, 9, 12} in descriptive form, and give the set-builder form of {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}.

Step 1: Look at 3, 6, 9, 12. Each number is 3 × 1, 3 × 2, 3 × 3, 3 × 4.

Step 2: So they are the first four multiples of 3.

Step 3: Descriptive form: D = the set of the first four multiples of the number 3.

Step 4: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 are odd numbers from 1 to 9.

Step 5: Set-builder form: {x / x ∈ O, 1 ≤ x ≤ 9}.

Remember

  • O = {a, e, i, o, u} is the set of vowels of the English alphabet.
  • W = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8} is the set of whole numbers up to 8.
  • M = {March, May} is the set of months whose names begin with M.
  • The first five even numbers 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 are written as {x / x ∈ E ∧ 2 ≤ x ≤ 10}.
  • All natural numbers are written as {x / x ∈ N}.

mcqs.q: What is the descriptive form of D = {3, 6, 9, 12}?
options: The set of the first four multiples of 3
The set of the first four even numbers
The set of odd numbers up to 12
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the set of the first four multiples of 3. 3, 6, 9 and 12 are 3×1, 3×2, 3×3 and 3×4. The lesson point is: read the pattern of the members first, then write it in words.

mcqs.q: O = {a, e, i, o, u} is the set of what?
options: First five letters of the alphabet
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the vowels of the English alphabet. a, e, i, o and u are exactly the five vowels. In descriptive form we name the common property shared by all members.

mcqs.q: W = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8} in descriptive form is:
options: The set of natural numbers up to 8
The set of whole numbers up to 8
The set of integers up to 8
The set of first eight natural numbers
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the set of whole numbers up to 8. The set starts from 0, and whole numbers start from 0 while natural numbers start from 1. That starting number decides the name.

mcqs.q: M = {March, May} is best described as:
options: The set of months with 31 days
The set of months beginning with T
The set of months of the year beginning with M
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the set of months beginning with M. March and May are the only months in the list and both begin with M. Descriptive form must fit every member and no extra member.

mcqs.q: The set-builder form of the first five even numbers is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {x / x ∈ E ∧ 2 ≤ x ≤ 10}. The first five even numbers are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, so x is even and lies from 2 to 10. E stands for even numbers in set-builder form.

mcqs.q: The set-builder form of {1, 3, 5, 7, 9} is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {x / x ∈ O, 1 ≤ x ≤ 9}. 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 are odd numbers, so we use O, and the smallest is 1 and the largest is 9. Both the type and the limits must be correct.

mcqs.q: The first ten whole numbers 0 to 9 in set-builder form are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {x / x ∈ W ∧ 0 ≤ x ≤ 9}. Whole numbers start at 0, and the first ten are 0, 1, 2, ..., 9. W is used because 0 is included.

mcqs.q: The set-builder form of {−2, −1, 0, 1, 2} is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {x / x ∈ Z ∧ −2 ≤ x ≤ 2}. The set has negative numbers, zero and positive numbers, so these are integers, Z. The limits are −2 and 2.

mcqs.q: All natural numbers in set-builder form are written as:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {x / x ∈ N}. N is the symbol for the set of all natural numbers 1, 2, 3, ... with no upper limit. No limit is needed because the set goes on without end.

mcqs.q: The members of B in Practical Work are the distinct letters of which word?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the word خوبصورت, as given in the book. In a set each distinct letter is written only once, even if it appears more than once in the word. This is the same rule used for the letters of Pakistan in Exercise 1.1.

lessons.title: Exercise 1.1 — What Is a Set? The Three Forms of a Set
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

Every set can be written in three forms. Descriptive form uses words. Tabular form, also called roster form, lists all members inside { } separated by commas. Set-builder form uses a rule, like {x / x ∈ N ∧ x ≤ 5}. In this exercise you change a set from one form to another.

Formula / Rule

Tabular form: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} — list each member once; order does not matter.

Set-builder form: {x / condition on x} — read / as such that, ∈ as belongs to, ∧ as and.

Natural numbers N start from 1. Whole numbers W start from 0. Integers Z include negative numbers, 0 and positive numbers.

Worked Example

Example: Write A = {x / x ∈ N ∧ x ≤ 5} in tabular form.

Step 1: N means natural numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, ...

Step 2: The condition x ≤ 5 means keep only numbers up to 5.

Step 3: The numbers that satisfy both are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

Step 4: Tabular form: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}.

Remember

  • F = {1, 2, 5, 10} is the set of factors of 10, and G = {1, 3, 5, 15} is the set of factors of 15.
  • J = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11} is the set of prime numbers up to 11.
  • In the word Pakistan, a comes twice but is written once: {p, a, k, i, s, t, n}.
  • Dots ... mean the pattern continues, e.g. {2, 4, 6, 8, ...} is the set of even natural numbers.
  • C = {−3, −2, −1, 0, 1} is the set of integers less than 2 and greater than −4.

mcqs.q: N = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, ...} in descriptive form is:
options: The set of all natural numbers
The set of first six natural numbers
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the set of all natural numbers. The dots ... show the set continues without end, starting from 1. Natural numbers start from 1, not from 0.

mcqs.q: E = {2, 4, 6, 8} is the set of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the first four even numbers. 2, 4, 6 and 8 can all be divided by 2 and there are four of them. Count the members and check the pattern before writing the description.

mcqs.q: F = {1, 2, 5, 10} is the set of:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the factors of 10. 10 is exactly divisible by 1, 2, 5 and 10, and by no other counting number. Factors divide the number exactly; multiples are the number times 1, 2, 3, ...

mcqs.q: The tabular form of the first seven natural numbers is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}. Natural numbers start from 1, so the first seven are 1 to 7. Whole numbers would start from 0 instead.

mcqs.q: The set of integers less than 2 and greater than −4 in tabular form is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {−3, −2, −1, 0, 1}. Greater than −4 means −3 is the first, and less than 2 means 1 is the last; −4 and 2 themselves are not included. Read less than and greater than carefully at both ends.

mcqs.q: The letters of the word Pakistan as a set are:
options: {p, a, k, i, s, t, a, n}
{p, a, k, i, s, t, n}
{P, a, k, i, s, t, a, n} with a twice
{p, k, i, s, t, n} without a
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {p, a, k, i, s, t, n}. The letter a appears twice in Pakistan but in a set every member is written only once. Never repeat a member in tabular form.

mcqs.q: The set-builder form of A = {1, 2, 3, ..., 10} is:
options: {x / x is a river of Pakistan}
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {x / x ∈ N ∧ x ≤ 10}. The members are natural numbers from 1 to 10, so x ∈ N with the limit x ≤ 10. The type N and the limit must both match the listed members.

mcqs.q: B = {y / y ∈ E ∧ 4 ≤ y ≤ 20} in tabular form is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20}. y ∈ E means y is even, and 4 ≤ y ≤ 20 keeps only the even numbers from 4 to 20. Both ends 4 and 20 are included because of ≤.

mcqs.q: D = {z / z ∈ W ∧ z < 5} in tabular form is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}. W means whole numbers starting from 0, and z < 5 means 5 is not included. Whole numbers include 0, which is the key difference from natural numbers.

mcqs.q: The set-builder form of L = {4, 8, 12, 16, 20, ...} is:
options: {x / x is an odd natural number}
{x / x is a multiple of the number 4}
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {x / x is a multiple of the number 4}. 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 are 4×1, 4×2, 4×3, 4×4, 4×5 and the dots show they continue. Multiples go on without end unless a limit is given.

lessons.title: Exercise 1.2 — Union, Intersection and Difference of Sets
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

Here you join or compare two sets. Union ∪ collects all members of both sets. Intersection ∩ keeps only the common members. Difference − keeps the members of the first set that are not in the second set. A member that appears in both sets is written only once in the union.

Formula / Rule

A ∪ B = {all members of A and B, each written once}

A ∩ B = {members common to both A and B}

A − B = {members of A that are not in B}

Worked Example

Example: A = {4, 5, 6} and B = {5, 6, 7, 8}. Find A − B and B − A.

Step 1: For A − B, start with A = {4, 5, 6}.

Step 2: Remove 5 and 6 because they are also in B.

Step 3: A − B = {4}.

Step 4: For B − A, start with B = {5, 6, 7, 8} and remove 5 and 6.

Step 5: B − A = {7, 8}. Note A − B and B − A are different.

Remember

  • A ∪ { } = A: joining with the empty set changes nothing.
  • If there is no common member, A ∩ B = { } = ∅.
  • Union and intersection give the same answer in any order, but difference does not: A − B ≠ B − A in general.
  • For whole numbers W and natural numbers N: W − N = {0} and N − W = { }.

mcqs.q: If A = {4, 5} and B = {4, 6, 8, 9}, then A ∪ B is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {4, 5, 6, 8, 9}. Union collects every member of both sets, and 4, which is in both, is written only once. Never write a member twice in a set.
The correct answer is {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8}. Take all of A, then add 6 and 8 from B because 2 and 4 are already in A. 7 is in neither set, so it is not included.

mcqs.q: X is the first four odd numbers and Y is the first 3 multiples of 3. X ∪ Y is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9}. X = {1, 3, 5, 7} and Y = {3, 6, 9}; joining them and writing 3 once gives the answer. First write both sets in tabular form, then do the operation.

mcqs.q: If A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 6, 9, 12}, then A ∩ B is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {3}. Intersection keeps only members common to both sets, and 3 is the only number in both A and B. All other members belong to only one set.

mcqs.q: If P = {a, b, c, d} and Q = {a, e, i, o, u}, then P ∩ Q is:
options: {a, b, c, d, e, i, o, u}
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {a}. The letter a is the only member present in both P and Q. Intersection is always the common part only.

mcqs.q: A is the set of integers and B is the set of positive integers. A ∩ B is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is B, the positive integers {1, 2, 3, ...}. Every positive integer is an integer, so all of B is common to both sets. When one set lies inside the other, the intersection is the smaller set.

mcqs.q: If A = {4, 5, 6} and B = {5, 6, 7, 8}, then A − B is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {4}. A − B keeps members of A that are not in B; 5 and 6 are in B so they are removed, leaving only 4. Difference always starts from the first set.

mcqs.q: For the same A = {4, 5, 6} and B = {5, 6, 7, 8}, B − A is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {7, 8}. B − A keeps members of B that are not in A; removing 5 and 6 from B leaves 7 and 8. This shows A − B and B − A are usually different.

mcqs.q: If A = {1, 3, 5, 9, 11} and B = {1, 3, 5, 7, 11}, then A − B and B − A are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is A − B = {9} and B − A = {7}. Only 9 is in A but not in B, and only 7 is in B but not in A. The common members 1, 3, 5, 11 disappear from both differences.

mcqs.q: If A = {1, 2, 3}, B = { } and C = {2, 3}, then (A ∪ B) ∪ C is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {1, 2, 3}. A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3} ∪ { } = {1, 2, 3}, and then ∪ C adds nothing new. Union with the empty set leaves a set unchanged.

lessons.title: Exercise 1.3 — Disjoint and Overlapping Sets
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

Two sets can be disjoint or overlapping. Disjoint sets have no member in common. Overlapping sets have some members in common, but neither set is fully inside the other. To decide, first find the intersection: if it is empty, the sets are disjoint; if it is not empty, check whether one set is a subset of the other.

Formula / Rule

Disjoint sets: A ∩ B = { } = ∅

Overlapping sets: A ∩ B ≠ ∅, and A ⊄ B and B ⊄ A

If every member of A is in B, then A ⊆ B and the pair is neither disjoint nor overlapping.

Worked Example

Example: W = {0, 1, 2, 3} and N = {1, 2, 3, 4}. Disjoint or overlapping?

Step 1: Find the common members: 1, 2 and 3 are in both sets.

Step 2: The intersection is not empty, so the sets are not disjoint.

Step 3: 0 is in W but not in N, and 4 is in N but not in W, so neither set is a subset of the other.

Step 4: Therefore W and N are overlapping sets.

Remember

  • C = {a, e, i, o, u} and D = {p, q, r} are disjoint — letters in one, different letters in the other, nothing common.
  • N = {a, e, i, o, u} and G = {h, o, c, k, y} overlap in only one member, o — one common member is enough for overlapping.
  • A = natural numbers 10 to 40 and W = whole numbers up to 40: A ⊆ W, so this pair is neither disjoint nor overlapping.
  • Even numbers and multiples of 5 overlap in 10, 20, 30, ...

mcqs.q: F and M have no common member, F ∩ M = { }. F and M are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is disjoint sets. Disjoint means the intersection is empty — there is no member common to both sets. F has shapes and M has names of things, so nothing is shared.

The correct answer is overlapping sets. They share 1, 2 and 3, but 0 is only in W and 4 is only in N, so neither is a subset of the other. Shared members plus members outside both ways means overlapping.

mcqs.q: C = {a, e, i, o, u} and D = {p, q, r} are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is disjoint sets. Although both sets contain letters, no letter is common to both: C ∩ D = { }. Disjoint is about common members, not about the type of objects.

options: N is a subset of M
mcqs.why: The correct answer is overlapping sets. They share 6, 8 and 12, but 1 is in N only and 14 is in M only, so neither set is inside the other. That is exactly the definition of overlapping.

mcqs.q: A = natural numbers from 10 to 40 and W = whole numbers up to 40. This pair is:
options: Neither — A is a subset of W
mcqs.why: The correct answer is neither — A is a subset of W. Every member of A is in W, so A ⊆ W; they have common members so they are not disjoint, and overlapping needs neither set to be a subset. Always check the subset case before calling a pair overlapping.

mcqs.q: E = {2, 4, 6, ...} (even numbers) and O = {5, 10, 15, ...} (multiples of 5) are:
options: E is a subset of O
mcqs.why: The correct answer is overlapping sets. Their common members are 10, 20, 30, ..., but 2 is in E only and 5 is in O only. Even multiples of 5 form the common part.

options: F is a subset of A
mcqs.why: The correct answer is disjoint sets. No number appears in both sets, so F ∩ A = { }. With an empty intersection the pair must be disjoint.

options: C is a subset of H
mcqs.why: The correct answer is overlapping sets. They share 3, 5 and 9, but 2 is in H only and 11 is in C only, so neither contains the other. A few common members with extras on both sides means overlapping.

mcqs.q: N = {a, e, i, o, u} and G = {h, o, c, k, y} are:
options: N is a subset of G
mcqs.why: The correct answer is overlapping sets. They share only one member, o, and one common member is enough — the intersection is not empty. Since a is not in G and h is not in N, neither is a subset of the other.

options: Q is a subset of E
mcqs.why: The correct answer is disjoint sets. Q contains shapes and E contains numbers, so there is no common member and Q ∩ E = { }. Different kinds of objects with nothing shared are disjoint.

lessons.title: Exercise 1.4 — Universal Set and Complement of a Set
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

The universal set U contains all the members under discussion. The complement of a set A, written A′, is everything in U that is not in A. Think of it as: take U and remove A. A set and its complement together make the whole U, and they share no member.

Formula / Rule

A′ = U − A

A ∪ A′ = U

A ∩ A′ = ∅

U′ = ∅ and ∅′ = U

Worked Example

Example: U = {a, b, c, d, e, f} and A = {a, e, f}. Find A′.

Step 1: Write U fully: {a, b, c, d, e, f}.

Step 2: Remove the members of A: remove a, e and f.

Step 3: The members left are b, c and d.

Step 4: So A′ = {b, c, d}. Check: A ∪ A′ = {a, b, c, d, e, f} = U. ✓

Remember

  • Complement always depends on U — the same A can have a different A′ if U changes.
  • U = {1, ..., 10}, E = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10} gives E′ = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}: the complement of the evens is the odds.
  • U ∩ U′ = ∅ because U′ is empty.
  • U ∪ U′ = U because joining U with the empty set gives U.

mcqs.q: If U = {a, b, c, d, e, f} and A = {a, e, f}, then A′ is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {b, c, d}. A′ = U − A: remove a, e and f from U and b, c, d remain. The complement is everything in U that is not in A.

mcqs.q: For the same U and A, A ∪ A′ equals:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is U. A set together with its complement covers the whole universal set: {a, e, f} ∪ {b, c, d} = {a, b, c, d, e, f} = U. This rule A ∪ A′ = U holds for every set.

mcqs.q: For the same U and A, A ∩ A′ equals:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is ∅, the empty set. A and A′ have no member in common, because every member of U is either in A or in A′, never in both. So A ∩ A′ = ∅ always.

mcqs.q: U′ is always equal to:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is ∅. U′ = U − U, and removing everything from U leaves nothing. The complement of the universal set is the empty set.

mcqs.q: ∅′ is always equal to:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is U. ∅′ = U − ∅, and removing nothing from U leaves the whole of U. The complement of the empty set is the universal set.
The correct answer is {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}. Removing the even numbers from 1 to 10 leaves the odd numbers. Here the complement of the evens inside U is exactly the odds.
The correct answer is {0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12}. U runs from 0 to 12; removing the odd numbers in P leaves 0 and the even numbers. Note 0 and 12 are in U, so they appear in P′.

mcqs.q: If U = {u, v, w, x, y, z} and B = {x, y, z}, then B′ is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {u, v, w}. B′ = U − B: remove x, y and z from U and u, v, w remain. Then B′ ∪ B = U, as a check.
The correct answer is {4, 8, 9, 10}. From 1 to 10, remove 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7; the numbers left are 4, 8, 9 and 10. List U in order and cross out A to avoid missing a number.

mcqs.q: U ∩ U′ equals:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is ∅. U′ = ∅, so U ∩ ∅ = ∅ — there is no member common to U and the empty set. Any intersection with the empty set is empty.

lessons.title: Exercise 1.5 — Laws of Sets: Verifying Equalities
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

In this exercise you verify laws by working out both sides and showing they give the same set. Union and intersection are commutative — the order does not matter — and associative — brackets do not matter. Difference is not commutative. You also verify the complement laws, including De Morgan-style laws: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′.

Formula / Rule

A ∪ B = B ∪ A and A ∩ B = B ∩ A (commutative)

(A ∪ B) ∪ C = A ∪ (B ∪ C) and (A ∩ B) ∩ C = A ∩ (B ∩ C) (associative)

(A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′

But A − B ≠ B − A in general.

Worked Example

Example: A = {1, −2, −3}, B = {−1, −4, −5, −6}. Verify A ∪ B = B ∪ A.

Step 1: Left side: A ∪ B = {1, −2, −3} ∪ {−1, −4, −5, −6} = {1, −2, −3, −1, −4, −5, −6}.

Step 2: Right side: B ∪ A = {−1, −4, −5, −6} ∪ {1, −2, −3}.

Step 3: The right side contains exactly the same members, only in a different order.

Step 4: Order does not matter in a set, so A ∪ B = B ∪ A is verified. ✓

Remember

  • To verify, always calculate the left side and the right side separately, then compare members.
  • B ∩ C = {−1, −4} for B = {−1, −4, −5, −6}, C = {0, −1, −2, −3, −4}, and C ∩ B gives the same — intersection is commutative.
  • B − C = {−5, −6} but C − B = {0, −2, −3} — difference is not commutative.
  • With U = {10, ..., 20}, A = {10, 12, 14, 16, 18}: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ = {17, 19, 20}.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is {1, −2, −3, −1, −4, −5, −6}. The two sets have no common member, so the union simply joins all seven members. B ∪ A gives the same set, which verifies commutativity of union.
The correct answer is {−5, −6}. Remove from B the members that are also in C, namely −1 and −4; −5 and −6 remain. Difference keeps only the first set's own members.

mcqs.q: For the same B and C, C − B is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {0, −2, −3}. Remove from C the members that are also in B, namely −1 and −4; 0, −2 and −3 remain. Since B − C = {−5, −6} is different, B − C ≠ C − B is verified.
The correct answer is {−2, −3}. These are the members present in both A and C; 1 is only in A and 0, −1, −4 are only in C. Intersection is the common part only.
The correct answer is { }, the empty set. A and B have no member in common, so their intersection is empty. B ∩ A is also empty, so A ∩ B = B ∩ A is still verified.
The correct answer is {11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 20}. U runs from 10 to 20; removing the five members of A leaves six members, including 20. Always write out the full U before finding a complement.
The correct answer is {16, 17, 18, 19, 20}. Removing 10 to 15 from U = 10 to 20 leaves 16 to 20. Then B ∩ B′ = ∅, which verifies that a set and its complement never overlap.
The correct answer is {10, 12, 14}. These three numbers are in both A and B; 16 and 18 are only in A, and 11, 13, 15 are only in B. This intersection is used to verify (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′.

mcqs.q: For the same U, A and B, (A ∪ B)′ is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {17, 19, 20}. A ∪ B = {10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 18}, and removing these from U leaves 17, 19 and 20. It equals A′ ∩ B′, verifying the law (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′.

mcqs.q: Which statement is TRUE for all sets?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is A ∪ B = B ∪ A. Union is commutative, so the order never changes the result. Difference is not commutative, and (A ∪ B)′ equals A′ ∩ B′, not A′ ∪ B′.

lessons.title: Exercise 1.6 — Venn Diagrams for Set Operations
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

A Venn diagram draws sets as circles. The universal set U is a rectangle around the circles. Disjoint sets are drawn as separate circles. Overlapping sets are drawn as circles that cross, and the crossing part is the intersection. You show an operation by shading the region it stands for.

Formula / Rule

Shade both circles fully for A ∪ B; shade only the common middle part for A ∩ B.

Shade only the part of A outside B for A − B; shade everything in the rectangle outside A for A′.

If the sets are disjoint: A ∩ B = ∅, A − B = A and B − A = B.

Worked Example

Example: Y = {1, 2, 3, ..., 12} and Z = {2, 4, 6, ..., 16}. Find Y ∩ Z and Y − Z by Venn diagram.

Step 1: The common members are {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12}, so draw overlapping circles.

Step 2: Shade only the middle part: Y ∩ Z = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12}.

Step 3: Shade the part of Y outside Z: Y − Z = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11}.

Step 4: The part of Z outside Y is Z − Y = {14, 16}.

Remember

  • U = {8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16}, A = {8, 10, 12, 14, 16}, B = {8, 15}: A ∩ B = {8} and (A ∪ B)′ = {11, 13}.
  • For disjoint A = {1, 3, 5, 7} and B = {2, 4, 6, 8}: A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}.
  • A′ ∪ A shades the whole rectangle and equals U.
  • B′ ∩ B has no region to shade and equals ∅.

mcqs.q: A = {1, 3, 5, 7} and B = {2, 4, 6, 8} are disjoint. In the Venn diagram they are drawn as:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is two separate circles. Disjoint sets have no common member, so there is no crossing part to draw. Their intersection has no region to shade.

mcqs.q: For disjoint A = {1, 3, 5, 7} and B = {2, 4, 6, 8}, A ∪ B is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}. In the diagram both circles are shaded fully, so the union contains every member of both sets. Nothing is common, so nothing is repeated.

mcqs.q: For the same disjoint A and B, A − B is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is A itself, {1, 3, 5, 7}. No member of A is in B, so nothing is removed from A. For disjoint sets, A − B = A and B − A = B.

mcqs.q: W = {a, b, c} and X = {u, v, w}. W ∩ X is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is { } = ∅. The sets share no member — note w in X is a letter, not the set W. With separate circles there is no common region to shade.
The correct answer is {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12}. These even numbers up to 12 are in both sets, so they form the shaded middle part of the overlapping circles. Numbers above 12 are in Z only.

mcqs.q: For the same Y and Z, Z − Y is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {14, 16}. Z goes up to 16, and 14 and 16 are the members of Z that are not in Y, which stops at 12. In the diagram this is the part of the Z circle outside Y.
The correct answer is {11, 13, 15}. A′ is the part of the rectangle outside the A circle: remove 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 from U. Note 15 is in A′ even though it belongs to B.

mcqs.q: For the same U, A and B = {8, 15}, A − B is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {10, 12, 14, 16}. A and B share only 8, so removing B from A removes just 8. In the diagram, shade the part of the A circle that does not overlap B.

mcqs.q: For the same U, A and B, (A ∪ B)′ is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {11, 13}. A ∪ B = {8, 10, 12, 14, 15, 16}, and the part of the rectangle outside both circles is {11, 13}. That outside region is exactly the complement of the union.

mcqs.q: For the same U, A and B, A′ ∩ B is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {15}. A′ = {11, 13, 15} and B = {8, 15}, so the only common member is 15. In the diagram this is the part of the B circle lying outside A.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 1 — Sets: Mixed Practice
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

This review mixes everything from Unit 1: the three forms of a set, union, intersection, difference, complement, disjoint and overlapping sets, the laws of sets, and Venn diagrams. The method is always the same: write the sets out fully first, then do one operation at a time, step by step.

Formula / Rule

A′ = U − A, A ∪ A′ = U, A ∩ A′ = ∅

(A ∪ B)′ and (A ∩ B)′: first do the part in brackets, then take the complement in U.

Disjoint: A ∩ B = ∅. Overlapping: some common members, neither set a subset of the other.

Worked Example

Example: U = {1, 2, 3, ..., 12}, A = {1, 2, 3, 10}, B = {2, 4, 6, ..., 12}. Find (A ∩ C)′ where C = {1, 3, 5, ..., 11}.

Step 1: First find A ∩ B check later; for (A ∩ C)′, find A ∩ C = {1, 2, 3, 10} ∩ {1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11} = {1, 3}.

Step 2: Now take the complement in U: (A ∩ C)′ = U − {1, 3}.

Step 3: Remove 1 and 3 from {1, 2, ..., 12}.

Step 4: (A ∩ C)′ = {2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12}.

Remember

  • The three forms are descriptive, tabular (roster) and set-builder.
  • With U = {1, ..., 12} as above, (B ∪ C)′ = ∅ because B ∪ C = U.
  • If A = {x, y, z} and B = {y, z, x}, the sets are equal, so A − B = ∅.
  • If every member of X is in Y, draw the X circle inside the Y circle: X ∪ Y = Y and X ∩ Y = X.

mcqs.q: The three forms of expressing a set are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is descriptive, tabular and set-builder. These are the three ways to write the same set: in words, as a list, and by a rule. Union and intersection are operations, not forms.

mcqs.q: The first five whole numbers in tabular form are:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}. Whole numbers start from 0, so the first five are 0 to 4. Natural numbers would start from 1 instead.

mcqs.q: A = {a, b, c, d, ...} in descriptive form is:
options: The set of first four letters
The set of the letters of the English alphabet
The set of letters of Pakistan
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the set of the letters of the English alphabet. The dots show the letters continue from a through the whole alphabet. Without the dots it would be only four letters.
The correct answer is {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12}. Join all members of A and B, writing 2 and 10 only once. The odd numbers 5, 7, 9, 11 are in neither set, so U is not the answer.

mcqs.q: For the same A and B, A ∩ B is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {2}, as worked in the book. Intersection keeps only the members common to both sets, found by comparing A = {1, 2, 3, 10} with B = {2, 4, 6, ..., 12} member by member. Always do this comparison in order so no common member is missed.

mcqs.q: For the same U, A and B, A − B is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {1, 3, 10}, as worked in the book. A − B keeps the members of A that remain after removing the shared members found in the intersection step. Difference always starts from the first set, A.

mcqs.q: If U = {a, b, c, d, e} and A = {a, b, c}, then A′ is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {d, e}. A′ = U − A: remove a, b and c from U, leaving d and e. This is the book's own multiple-choice question, and its answer is option (d).

mcqs.q: If A = {l, m, n} and B = {l, m, n, o}, then B − A is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {o}. B − A removes l, m and n from B, and only o remains. Difference starts from the first-named set, here B.

mcqs.q: If P = {1, 2, 3} and Q = {2, 3, 4}, then P ∩ Q is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is {2, 3}. Both 2 and 3 are in P as well as in Q, so they form the intersection. 1 is only in P and 4 is only in Q.

mcqs.q: If A = {x, y, z} and B = {y, z, x}, then A − B is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is ∅. A and B have exactly the same members, only in a different order, so the sets are equal and nothing is left after removing B from A. Order never matters in a set.

lessons.title: Exercise 2.1 — What Are Rational Numbers?
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

A rational number is any number that can be written as a fraction p/q.

Here p and q are integers and q is not zero. Integers, whole numbers and natural numbers are all rational numbers, because any such number a can be written as a/1.

For example, 0/5 = 0 is rational, 0 = 0/1 is rational, and 2 1/5 = 11/5 is rational. But 5/0 is NOT rational, because we can never divide by zero.

Formula / Rule

Rational number = p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0

To find a rational number between two numbers, take their average: (first number + second number) / 2

Worked Example

Question: Write a rational number between 2 and 3.

Step 1: Add the two numbers: 2 + 3 = 5.

Step 2: Divide by 2: 5/2 = 2 1/2.

Step 3: Check: 2 < 5/2 < 3, so 5/2 lies between 2 and 3.

Showing Numbers on the Number Line

First change the fraction to a mixed number to see between which two whole numbers it lies. For example, 7/2 = 3 1/2 lies between 3 and 4, 11/3 = 3 2/3 lies between 3 and 4, and 15/8 = 1 7/8 lies between 1 and 2.

Negative numbers go to the left of zero. For example, -2/5 lies between 0 and -1, and -12/5 = -2 2/5 lies between -2 and -3.

Then divide that part of the line into equal parts equal to the denominator and count the numerator parts.

Remember

  • In p/q, q can be any non-zero integer. It does not have to be even. In 1/3, q = 3.
  • p and q are integers, not only natural numbers. In -2/3, p = -2.
  • There are infinitely many rational numbers between any two numbers, not only one.
  • On a number line in this exercise, x = 2, y = 2 1/6 and z = 4.

mcqs.q: Is 0/5 a rational number?
options: Yes, because the denominator 5 is not zero
No, because the numerator is zero
Yes, only if the denominator is zero
mcqs.why:
0/5 is rational because it is in the form p/q with q = 5, which is not zero.
0/5 = 0, and 0 itself can also be written as 0/1.
A zero numerator is allowed; a zero denominator is not.

mcqs.q: Why is 5/0 NOT a rational number?
options: Because the denominator is zero and division by zero is not possible
Because the numerator is bigger than the denominator
mcqs.why:
In a rational number p/q, q must not be zero.
In 5/0 the denominator is zero, and no number can be divided by zero.
So 5/0 is not a rational number.

mcqs.q: Is 0 a rational number?
options: No, because it has no fraction form
Yes, because 0 = 0/1 with a non-zero denominator
mcqs.why:
0 can be written in the form p/q as 0/1.
The denominator 1 is not zero, so this fits the definition.
Therefore the statement '0 is not a rational number' is false.

mcqs.q: In a rational number p/q, what can q be?
mcqs.why:
q can be any integer that is not zero, for example q = 3 in 1/3.
It does not have to be even, as 1/3 shows.
Only q = 0 is forbidden.

mcqs.q: What is a rational number between 2 and 3, found by taking the average?
mcqs.why:
Average of 2 and 3 = (2 + 3) / 2 = 5/2.
5/2 = 2 1/2, and 2 < 5/2 < 3.
So 5/2 lies between 2 and 3.

mcqs.q: How many rational numbers are there between 2 and 3?
mcqs.why:
There are infinitely many rational numbers between 2 and 3.
The book gives examples 5/2, 9/4 and 11/4, all between 2 and 3.
So 'there is only one' is false.

mcqs.q: 7/2 lies between which two whole numbers on the number line?
mcqs.why:
7/2 = 3 1/2.
A number equal to 3 and a half lies between 3 and 4.
Divide the part between 3 and 4 into 2 equal parts to mark it.

mcqs.q: -2/5 lies between which two numbers on the number line?
mcqs.why:
-2/5 = -0.4, which is negative and less than 1 in size.
Negative fractions between 0 and -1 lie in that part of the line.
Divide the part between 0 and -1 into 5 parts and take 2 parts from 0.

mcqs.q: 15/8 written as a mixed number is:
mcqs.why:
15 divided by 8 gives 1 whole with remainder 7.
So 15/8 = 1 7/8.
It lies between 1 and 2 on the number line.

mcqs.q: Why is every integer a rational number?
options: Because every integer has a reciprocal
Because every integer a can be written as a/1
Because every integer is a fraction already
mcqs.why:
Take any integer a. It can be written as a/1.
The denominator 1 is not zero, so it is in the form p/q.
This is why all integers, whole numbers and natural numbers are rational.

lessons.title: Exercise 2.2 — Adding, Subtracting, Multiplying and Dividing
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

In this exercise we do +, -, × and ÷ with rational numbers, and we find reciprocals and inverses.

The reciprocal is found by turning the fraction upside down. The additive inverse is found by changing the sign. The multiplicative inverse is the same as the reciprocal.

Formula / Rule

Reciprocal of a/b = b/a, and a number × its reciprocal = 1

For addition or subtraction with the same denominator: add or subtract only the numerators and keep the denominator

For different denominators: make the denominators the same using the LCM, then add or subtract

To divide: a/b ÷ c/d = a/b × d/c — change ÷ to × and turn the second fraction upside down

Worked Example

Question: Simplify 5/8 - 4/5.

Step 1: The denominators 8 and 5 are different, so find the LCM: LCM of 8 and 5 = 40.

Step 2: Write both fractions over 40: 5/8 = 25/40 and 4/5 = 32/40.

Step 3: Subtract the numerators: (25 - 32) / 40 = -7/40.

Answer: -7/40.

Other Question Types in This Exercise

  • Same denominator: 9/7 + 15/7 = 24/7 = 3 3/7, and 5/9 - 2/9 = 3/9 = 1/3. Subtracting a negative adds: 3/5 - (-7/5) = 10/5 = 2.
  • Reciprocals: reciprocal of 19/17 is 17/19, of -13 = -13/1 is -1/13, of 1/10 is 10, and of -6/25 is -25/6.
  • Inverses: for 17/15, additive inverse is -17/15 and multiplicative inverse is 15/17. For 0, additive inverse is 0 but there is NO multiplicative inverse.
  • Multiplication: multiply top by top and bottom by bottom, e.g. 5/8 × 3/2 = 15/16. Watch the signs: two negatives give a positive, e.g. -6/7 ÷ (-7/6) = 36/49.

Remember

  • 0 has no reciprocal and no multiplicative inverse, because 0 × anything = 0, never 1.
  • Always simplify the final answer, e.g. 51/42 = 17/14 = 1 3/14.
  • One negative sign in multiplication makes the answer negative; two negatives make it positive.

mcqs.q: What is the reciprocal of 19/17?
mcqs.why:
The reciprocal is found by interchanging numerator and denominator.
So the reciprocal of 19/17 is 17/19.
Check: (19/17) × (17/19) = 1.

mcqs.q: What is the reciprocal of -13?
mcqs.why:
Write -13 as -13/1 first.
Turning it upside down gives -1/13, and the sign stays negative.
Check: (-13) × (-1/13) = 1.

The denominators are the same (7), so add only the numerators.
(9 + 15) / 7 = 24/7.
24/7 simplifies as a mixed number to 3 3/7.

The denominators are the same, so subtract the numerators: (5 - 2) / 9 = 3/9.
Simplify 3/9 by dividing top and bottom by 3.
3/9 = 1/3.

Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding a positive one.
So 3/5 - (-7/5) = (3 + 7) / 5 = 10/5.
10/5 = 2.

The LCM of 8 and 5 is 40.
5/8 - 4/5 = (25 - 32) / 40 = -7/40.
The answer is negative because 25 is smaller than 32.

mcqs.q: What are the additive inverse and multiplicative inverse of 17/15?
mcqs.why:
The additive inverse changes the sign: -17/15, because 17/15 + (-17/15) = 0.
The multiplicative inverse is the reciprocal: 15/17, because (17/15) × (15/17) = 1.
So the pair is -17/15 and 15/17.

mcqs.q: What is the multiplicative inverse of -1/20?
mcqs.why:
The multiplicative inverse is the reciprocal: turn -1/20 upside down.
That gives -20/1 = -20, keeping the negative sign.
Check: (-1/20) × (-20) = 1.

mcqs.q: Which statement about 0 is true?
mcqs.why:
0 + 0 = 0, so the additive inverse of 0 is 0 itself.
But 0 × any number = 0, never 1.
So 0 has no multiplicative inverse (no reciprocal).

Change division to multiplication and invert the second fraction: 14/5 × 25/7.
(14 × 25) / (5 × 7) = 350/35.
350/35 = 10.

lessons.title: Exercise 2.3 — Properties and Ordering Rational Numbers
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

This exercise checks the big rules (properties) of rational numbers and teaches us to write rational numbers in ascending order (small to big) and descending order (big to small).

To verify a property, work out the left side and the right side separately. If LHS = RHS, the property is true.

Formula / Rule

Commutative: a + b = b + a and a × b = b × a — changing the order does not change the answer

Associative: a + (b + c) = (a + b) + c and a × (b × c) = (a × b) × c — changing the brackets does not change the answer

Distributive: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c and a × (b - c) = a × b - a × c

To compare fractions: make all denominators the same using the LCM, then compare the numerators

Worked Example

Question: Write 1/2, 2/3 and 8/9 in ascending order.

Step 1: Find the LCM of 2, 3 and 9: LCM = 18.

Step 2: Change each fraction: 1/2 = 9/18, 2/3 = 12/18, 8/9 = 16/18.

Step 3: Compare the numerators: 9 < 12 < 16.

Answer: 1/2 < 2/3 < 8/9.

Other Question Types in This Exercise

  • Commutative check: 2/3 + (-4/3) = -2/3 and (-4/3) + 2/3 = -2/3, and 4/7 × 2/5 = 8/35 both ways.
  • Associative check: 1/2 + (1/3 + 1/4) = 13/12 both ways, and 3/4 × (4/5 × 2/7) = 6/35 both ways.
  • Distributive check: 7/8 × (4/5 + 3/4) = 217/160 both ways, and 1/5 × (3/4 - 5/7) = 1/140 both ways.
  • Descending example: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 becomes 1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4, and 4/5, 1/10, 2/15 becomes 4/5 > 2/15 > 1/10.

Remember

  • Ascending means smallest first; descending means biggest first.
  • Never compare fractions with different denominators directly — first make the denominators equal.
  • Simplify fractions first when needed, e.g. 4/20 = 1/5 and 20/15 = 4/3.

mcqs.why:
Add the numerators over the same denominator: (2 - 4) / 3 = -2/3.
(-4/3) + 2/3 also gives -2/3.
Equal results verify the commutative property of addition.

Multiply numerator by numerator and denominator by denominator.
(4 × 2) / (7 × 5) = 8/35.
2/5 × 4/7 gives the same 8/35, verifying commutativity of multiplication.

First 1/3 + 1/4 = 7/12.
Then 1/2 + 7/12 = (6 + 7) / 12 = 13/12.
(1/2 + 1/3) + 1/4 also gives 13/12, so associativity of addition holds.

First 4/5 × 2/7 = 8/35.
Then 3/4 × 8/35 = 24/140 = 6/35.
The other grouping also gives 6/35, verifying associativity of multiplication.

First 3/4 - 5/7 = (21 - 20) / 28 = 1/28.
Then 1/5 × 1/28 = 1/140.
The distributed side 3/20 - 1/7 also equals 1/140.

mcqs.q: Write 1/2, 2/3, 8/9 in ascending order.
mcqs.why:
With LCM 18: 1/2 = 9/18, 2/3 = 12/18, 8/9 = 16/18.
The numerators go 9 < 12 < 16.
So ascending order is 1/2 < 2/3 < 8/9.

mcqs.q: Write 1/6, 3/4, 1/2 in ascending order.
mcqs.why:
With LCM 12: 1/6 = 2/12, 1/2 = 6/12, 3/4 = 9/12.
The numerators go 2 < 6 < 9.
So ascending order is 1/6 < 1/2 < 3/4.

mcqs.q: Write 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 in descending order.
mcqs.why:
With LCM 12: 1/2 = 6/12, 1/3 = 4/12, 1/4 = 3/12.
The numerators go 6 > 4 > 3.
So descending order is 1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4.

mcqs.q: Write 4/5, 1/10, 2/15 in descending order.
mcqs.why:
With LCM 30: 4/5 = 24/30, 2/15 = 4/30, 1/10 = 3/30.
The numerators go 24 > 4 > 3.
So descending order is 4/5 > 2/15 > 1/10.

mcqs.q: In (-1/2) + 1/3 = 1/3 + (-1/2), which property is used?
mcqs.why:
Only the order of the two numbers has changed.
The answer stays the same when the order changes.
That is the commutative property of addition.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 2 — Rational Numbers: Mixed Practice
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

This review mixes everything from Unit 2: the definition of rational numbers, inverses, all four operations, comparing numbers, the number line, and naming the properties.

Formula / Rule

A rational number is p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Examples: 3/4, -2/5, 7, 0

Additive inverse of a is -a, because a + (-a) = 0. Reciprocal of p/q is q/p, because (p/q) × (q/p) = 1

p/q + r/s = (ps + rq) / (qs), and (a/b) × (c/d) = ac / bd

The inverse operation of addition is subtraction, and the inverse operation of multiplication is division

Worked Example

Question: Solve 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6.

Step 1: Find the LCM of 2, 3 and 6: LCM = 6.

Step 2: Change each fraction: 1/2 = 3/6, 1/3 = 2/6, 1/6 = 1/6.

Step 3: Add the numerators: (3 + 2 + 1) / 6 = 6/6.

Answer: 1.

Other Question Types in This Exercise

  • Fill in the blanks: every improper fraction is a rational number; p/q and -p/q are additive inverses; 0 has no reciprocal; the multiplicative inverse is the reciprocal.
  • Comparing: use the LCM, e.g. 2/3 = 10/15 > 1/5 = 3/15, and 10/13 = 140/182 < 11/14 = 143/182. Any positive number is bigger than any negative number, e.g. 1/4 > -1/2.
  • Number line: 1 1/2 lies between 1 and 2, -1/4 lies between 0 and -1, and -1 4/5 lies between -1 and -2.
  • Division chains: work left to right, e.g. 8/21 ÷ 7/12 = 32/49 and (-1/100) ÷ (-1/10) = 1/10.
  • Naming properties: order changed = commutative, brackets changed = associative, one number multiplied over a sum or difference = distributive.

Remember

  • For -14: additive inverse is 14 and multiplicative inverse is -1/14.
  • For -11/27: additive inverse is 11/27 and multiplicative inverse is -27/11. The sign stays with the reciprocal.
  • For two negative fractions, compare carefully: -4/9 = -20/45 < -2/5 = -18/45.

mcqs.q: A number that can be shown in the form p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0, is called:
mcqs.why:
This is the exact definition from the review exercise.
Examples are 3/4, -2/5, 7 and 0.
So such a number is called a rational number.

mcqs.q: The additive inverse of 2/3 is:
mcqs.why:
The additive inverse changes the sign so the sum becomes zero.
2/3 + (-2/3) = 0.
So the additive inverse of 2/3 is -2/3.

mcqs.q: The multiplicative inverse of -4/7 is:
mcqs.why:
The multiplicative inverse is the reciprocal: turn -4/7 upside down.
That gives -7/4, keeping the negative sign.
Check: (-4/7) × (-7/4) = 1.

Make the denominators the same with LCM 6.
1/3 + 1/2 = (2 + 3) / 6 = 5/6.
So the correct answer is 5/6.

The denominators are the same, so add the numerators: (2 - 4) / 5.
That gives -2/5.
Adding a negative number makes the result smaller.

mcqs.q: The rational number 0 has no:
mcqs.why:
0 × any number = 0, never 1.
So no number can be the reciprocal of 0.
0 does have an additive inverse, which is 0 itself.

mcqs.q: p/q and -p/q are ___ inverses of each other.
mcqs.why:
p/q + (-p/q) = 0.
Two numbers whose sum is zero are additive inverses.
Their reciprocals would multiply to 1 instead.

mcqs.q: Find the additive and multiplicative inverses of -14.
mcqs.why:
Additive inverse: change the sign, giving 14, since -14 + 14 = 0.
Multiplicative inverse: reciprocal of -14/1 is -1/14, since (-14) × (-1/14) = 1.
So the pair is 14 and -1/14.

mcqs.q: Which sign goes between 2/3 and 1/5? 2/3 ___ 1/5
mcqs.why:
With LCM 15: 2/3 = 10/15 and 1/5 = 3/15.
10 is greater than 3.
So 2/3 > 1/5.

mcqs.q: Which sign goes between 10/13 and 11/14? 10/13 ___ 11/14
Which sign goes between -4/9 and -2/5? -4/9 ___ -2/5
mcqs.why:
With LCM 45: -4/9 = -20/45 and -2/5 = -18/45.
-20 is less than -18 (it is further left on the number line).
So -4/9 < -2/5.

Change ÷ to × and invert: (-1/100) × (-10/1) = 10/100.
Two negatives give a positive answer.
10/100 simplifies to 1/10.

Change ÷ to × and invert: 8/21 × 12/7 = 96/147.
Simplify 96/147 by dividing top and bottom by 3.
That gives the final answer 32/49.

options: Distributive property of multiplication over addition
mcqs.why:
One number, 2/3, is multiplied by a sum of two numbers.
The multiplication is distributed over each part of the sum.
That is the distributive property of multiplication over addition.

lessons.title: Exercise 3.1 — Converting Decimals to Fractions in Lowest Form
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

A decimal fraction is a fraction written with a decimal point, like 0.2, 0.15 or 3.125. Every terminating decimal can be written as a rational number — a fraction p/q. In this exercise you change decimals into fractions and then reduce them to lowest form.

The number of digits after the decimal point tells you the denominator. One digit means tenths, two digits mean hundredths, three digits mean thousandths, and so on.

Formula / Rule

Decimal to fraction: write the decimal digits over 10, 100, 1000, … according to the number of decimal places, then divide top and bottom by their common divisor until no common divisor is left.

Keep the minus sign with the fraction for negative decimals, for example −1.30 = −13/10.

Worked Example

Convert 0.75 into a rational number in lowest form.

Step 1: 0.75 has 2 decimal places, so write it over 100: 0.75 = 75/100.

Step 2: Divide 75 and 100 by 25.

Step 3: 75 ÷ 25 = 3 and 100 ÷ 25 = 4.

Step 4: Answer: 0.75 = 3/4.

More Types in This Exercise

  • One decimal place: 0.2 = 2/10 = 1/5, 0.6 = 6/10 = 3/5, 0.9 = 9/10.
  • Two decimal places: 0.15 = 15/100 = 3/20, 0.48 = 48/100 = 12/25, 0.95 = 95/100 = 19/20.
  • Numbers bigger than 1: 5.05 = 505/100 = 101/20 = 5 1/20, 5.60 = 560/100 = 28/5 = 5 3/5.
  • Three or more decimal places: 0.024 = 24/1000 = 3/125, 0.375 = 375/1000 = 3/8, 3.125 = 3125/1000 = 25/8.
  • Very small decimals: −0.005 = −5/1000 = −1/200, −0.00125 = −125/100000 = −1/800.

Remember

  • Count the decimal places first — that fixes the denominator.
  • Always simplify to lowest form; the exercise is not finished until you do.
  • A trailing zero does not change the value: 5.60 is the same as 5.6, but write it over 100 first if it helps.

mcqs.q: 0.2 in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 0.2 = 2/10 because there is 1 decimal place. Dividing 2 and 10 by 2 gives 1/5. This is the basic rule: count decimal places to choose the denominator, then simplify.

mcqs.q: 0.6 in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 0.6 = 6/10 with denominator 10 for one decimal place. Dividing top and bottom by 2 gives 3/5. The answer must be in lowest form, so 6/10 alone is not enough.

mcqs.q: 0.15 in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 0.15 has 2 decimal places, so 0.15 = 15/100. Dividing 15 and 100 by 5 gives 3/20. Two decimal places always start with denominator 100.

mcqs.q: 0.75 in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 0.75 = 75/100 because there are 2 decimal places. Dividing 75 and 100 by 25 gives 3/4. This is a very common decimal-fraction pair to remember.

mcqs.q: 0.48 in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 0.48 = 48/100 for 2 decimal places. Dividing 48 and 100 by 4 gives 12/25. 12 and 25 have no common divisor, so this is lowest form.

mcqs.q: 5.05 in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 5.05 = 505/100 because there are 2 decimal places. Dividing by 5 gives 101/20, which is also 5 1/20. Keep the whole part inside the fraction when you convert.

mcqs.q: 0.375 in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 0.375 has 3 decimal places, so 0.375 = 375/1000. Dividing 375 and 1000 by 125 gives 3/8. Three decimal places mean denominator 1000 to start.

mcqs.q: 3.125 in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 3.125 = 3125/1000 with 3 decimal places. Dividing by 125 gives 25/8, which is 3 1/8. The improper fraction 25/8 is the lowest-form answer.

mcqs.q: −0.005 in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: −0.005 = −5/1000 because there are 3 decimal places. Dividing 5 and 1000 by 5 gives −1/200. The minus sign stays with the fraction.

mcqs.q: 0.024 in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 0.024 = 24/1000 because there are 3 decimal places. Dividing 24 and 1000 by 8 gives 3/125. Always check for the biggest easy common divisor to reach lowest form quickly.

lessons.title: Practical Work — Terminating, Recurring and Rounding Decisions
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

This work has two jobs. First, divide a fraction and see if the decimal ends or goes on forever. Second, round long decimals to 2, 3 and 4 decimal places. Both jobs appear again and again in this unit.

If the decimal ends, it is terminating. If a digit or a group of digits keeps repeating forever, it is non-terminating and recurring, like 0.444… where 4 repeats.

Formula / Rule

Rounding rule: look at the digit just after the place you want to keep. If it is 5 or more, increase the last kept digit by 1. If it is less than 5, the last kept digit stays the same.

Worked Example

Round 2.421875 to 2, 3 and 4 decimal places.

Step 1: For 2 decimal places, look at the 3rd digit, which is 1. It is less than 5, so 2.421875 → 2.42.

Step 2: For 3 decimal places, look at the 4th digit, which is 8. It is 5 or more, so the 3rd digit 1 becomes 2: 2.421875 → 2.422.

Step 3: For 4 decimal places, look at the 5th digit, which is 7. It is 5 or more, so the 4th digit 8 becomes 9: 2.421875 → 2.4219.

More Types in This Work

  • Recurring by division: 4/9 = 0.444…, 25/7 = 3.571428… with group 571428 repeating, 3/11 = 0.2727… with group 27 repeating.
  • Rounding down: 0.83333 → 0.83 to 2 dp, 0.833 to 3 dp, 0.8333 to 4 dp.
  • Rounding up: 1.76794 → 1.77 to 2 dp, 1.768 to 3 dp, 1.7679 to 4 dp; 1.61538 → 1.62 to 2 dp.
  • Bigger numbers round the same way: 8.08547 → 8.09 to 2 dp, 15.47648 → 15.48 to 2 dp and 15.476 to 3 dp.

Remember

  • The dots … mean the decimal never ends.
  • Only look at ONE digit after the place you keep when rounding.
  • Write the same number of decimal places as asked, even if the last digit is 0.

mcqs.q: 4/9 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: 4 ÷ 9 = 0.444… and the digit 4 keeps repeating forever. A decimal that never ends with a repeating digit is non-terminating recurring. It does not stop at 0.44.

mcqs.q: 25/7 = 3.571428… The repeating group is:
mcqs.why: 25 ÷ 7 = 3.571428571428… and the block 571428 comes again and again. That whole block is the recurring group. Finding the full group is the key point of this example.

mcqs.q: 3/11 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: 3 ÷ 11 = 0.272727… where the group 27 repeats. So the decimal is non-terminating recurring. It is close to 0.27 but it never ends there.

mcqs.q: 2.421875 rounded to 2 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: For 2 decimal places look at the 3rd digit, which is 1. Since 1 is less than 5, the 2nd digit stays the same. So 2.421875 → 2.42.

mcqs.q: 2.421875 rounded to 3 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: For 3 decimal places look at the 4th digit, which is 8. Since 8 is 5 or more, the 3rd digit 1 increases to 2. So the answer is 2.422.

mcqs.q: 1.76794 rounded to 2 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: For 2 decimal places look at the 3rd digit, which is 7. Since 7 is 5 or more, the 2nd digit 6 increases to 7. So 1.76794 → 1.77.

mcqs.q: 0.9916667 rounded to 3 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: For 3 decimal places look at the 4th digit, which is 6. Since 6 is 5 or more, the 3rd digit 1 increases to 2. So 0.9916667 → 0.992.

mcqs.q: 1.61538 rounded to 2 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: For 2 decimal places look at the 3rd digit, which is 5. The rule says 5 or more means round up, so 1 becomes 2. So 1.61538 → 1.62.

mcqs.q: 8.08547 rounded to 2 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: For 2 decimal places look at the 3rd digit, which is 5. Since 5 means round up, the 2nd digit 8 increases to 9. So 8.08547 → 8.09.

mcqs.q: 6.98677 rounded to 3 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: For 3 decimal places look at the 4th digit, which is 7. Since 7 is 5 or more, the 3rd digit 6 increases to 7. So 6.98677 → 6.987.

lessons.title: Exercise 3.2 — Turning Fractions into Decimals
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

To turn a fraction into a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator. Sometimes the division ends exactly. Sometimes it never ends and a digit or group of digits repeats forever.

A decimal that ends is called terminating. A decimal that never ends with a repeating pattern is called non-terminating recurring.

Formula / Rule

Fraction to decimal: numerator ÷ denominator. If the remainder becomes 0, the decimal is terminating. If the same remainder keeps coming back, the decimal is non-terminating recurring.

Worked Example

Convert 2/11 into a decimal.

Step 1: Divide 2 by 11: 2 ÷ 11 = 0.18…

Step 2: Keep dividing: the digits 1 and 8 come again: 0.1818…

Step 3: The group 18 repeats forever, so the decimal never ends.

Step 4: Answer: 2/11 = 0.1818…, a recurring decimal with recurring group 18.

More Types in This Exercise

  • Single repeating digit: 7/3 = 2.333… (3 repeats), 10/3 = 3.333…, −13/9 = −1.444… (4 repeats), 14/9 = 1.555… (5 repeats).
  • Repeating digit after other digits: 11/6 = 1.8333… (3 repeats), 11/12 = 0.91666… (6 repeats).
  • Long repeating groups: 15/7 = 2.142857… (group 142857), 16/7 = 2.285714… (group 285714).
  • Terminating cases: 19/20 = 0.95, 15/8 = 1.875, 25/10 = 2.5, 4/25 = 0.16 — the division ends, nothing repeats.

Remember

  • Negative fractions give negative decimals, for example −13/9 = −1.444…
  • Write … to show the decimal continues.
  • Always say both the value and the type: terminating, or non-terminating recurring.

mcqs.q: 7/3 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: 7 ÷ 3 = 2.333… and the digit 3 repeats forever. So it is a non-terminating recurring decimal. It is not the same as the terminating decimal 2.3.

mcqs.q: In 11/6 = 1.8333…, the recurring digit is:
mcqs.why: 11 ÷ 6 = 1.8333… and after 1.8 the digit 3 keeps repeating. The recurring digit is the one that repeats forever, which is 3. The 8 appears only once.

mcqs.q: 19/20 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: 19 ÷ 20 = 0.95 and the division ends exactly. A decimal that ends is terminating and not recurring. This is Part II of the exercise, where some fractions do terminate.

mcqs.q: 15/8 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: 15 ÷ 8 = 1.875 and the remainder becomes 0, so the decimal ends. It is a terminating decimal, not recurring. Denominator 8 often gives a terminating decimal.

mcqs.q: 2/11 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: 2 ÷ 11 = 0.181818… where the group 18 repeats forever. So it is a recurring decimal with recurring group 18. Two digits repeat together as one group.

mcqs.q: 10/3 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: 10 ÷ 3 = 3.333… and the digit 3 repeats without end. So it is a recurring decimal. The whole part is 3 because 10 divided by 3 is more than 3.

mcqs.q: 11/12 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: 11 ÷ 12 = 0.91666… where 6 repeats after 0.91. So it is recurring with recurring digit 6. Only the repeating digit matters for the type, not the digits before it.

mcqs.q: 16/7 = 2.285714… The recurring group is:
mcqs.why: 16 ÷ 7 = 2.285714285714… and the block 285714 repeats. Fractions with denominator 7 often have a 6-digit repeating group. Here that group is 285714.

mcqs.q: 4/25 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: 4 ÷ 25 = 0.16 and the division ends exactly. So 4/25 is terminating and not recurring. It is one of the terminating examples in Part II.

mcqs.q: −13/9 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: −13 ÷ 9 = −1.444… where 4 repeats forever. The minus sign stays, so the decimal is negative. It is non-terminating recurring, just with a negative value.

lessons.title: Exercise 3.3 — Telling Terminating from Non-Terminating Without Dividing
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

You do NOT need to divide to know the type. First write the fraction in lowest form. Then break the denominator into prime factors. The primes in the denominator decide everything.

Formula / Rule

If the prime factors of the denominator (in lowest form) are only 2 and/or 5, the decimal is terminating. If the denominator has any other prime factor, like 3, 7 or 11, the decimal is non-terminating.

Important: simplify the fraction FIRST. For example 40/35 = 8/7, and only then look at denominator 7.

Worked Example

Without dividing, classify 17/20.

Step 1: 17/20 is already in lowest form.

Step 2: Break 20 into primes: 20 = 2 × 2 × 5.

Step 3: The primes are only 2 and 5.

Step 4: Answer: 17/20 is terminating, and in fact 17/20 = 0.85.

More Types in This Exercise

  • Only 5s: 12/25 (25 = 5 × 5, terminating, 0.48), 117/125 (125 = 5 × 5 × 5, terminating, 0.936).
  • Only 2s and 5s: −9/40 (40 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 5, terminating, −0.225).
  • Other primes present: 43/21 (21 = 3 × 7, non-terminating), 5/12 (12 = 2 × 2 × 3, non-terminating because of 3), 10/33 (33 = 3 × 11, non-terminating).
  • Simplify first: 55/75 = 11/15 (15 = 3 × 5, non-terminating), −96/100 = −24/25 (terminating), 111/96 = 37/32 (32 is only 2s, terminating), 372/400 = 93/100 (terminating).

Remember

  • Lowest form first — without it you can get the wrong answer.
  • Even one prime other than 2 or 5 makes it non-terminating.
  • The numerator does not decide the type; the denominator does.

mcqs.why: 12/25 is in lowest form and 25 = 5 × 5 has only prime 5. By the rule, only 2s and 5s means terminating. Indeed 12/25 = 0.48, which ends.
43/21 is in lowest form and 21 = 3 × 7 contains primes other than 2 or 5. So it is non-terminating: 43/21 = 2.047619… The numerator being prime does not matter.

mcqs.q: 5/12 is non-terminating because:
mcqs.why: 5/12 is in lowest form and 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. The prime 3 is neither 2 nor 5, so the decimal cannot terminate. Indeed 5/12 = 0.41666…
20 = 2 × 2 × 5 has only 2 and 5, so 17/20 is terminating. Dividing confirms it: 17/20 = 0.85. This is the standard worked pattern for this exercise.
40 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 has only 2 and 5, so the decimal terminates. The minus sign does not change the type. −9/40 = −0.225.

options: Non-terminating, because denominator 7 is neither 2 nor 5
mcqs.why: 5/7 is in lowest form and denominator 7 is a prime other than 2 or 5. So it must be non-terminating: 5/7 = 0.714285… A single wrong prime is enough.

mcqs.q: 40/35 simplifies to 8/7, so 40/35 is:
mcqs.why: You must simplify first: 40/35 = 8/7. Denominator 7 is neither 2 nor 5, so it is non-terminating: 1.142857… Looking at 35 before simplifying would give the wrong answer.

mcqs.q: −96/100 simplifies to −24/25, so it is:
mcqs.why: −96/100 = −24/25 in lowest form, and 25 = 5 × 5 has only 5. So it is terminating: −96/100 = −0.96. Simplifying first reveals the true denominator.

mcqs.q: 111/96 simplifies to 37/32. Since 32 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2, it is:
mcqs.why: In lowest form the denominator is 32, whose only prime factor is 2. Only 2s (and/or 5s) means terminating. Indeed 111/96 = 1.15625, which ends.

mcqs.q: 23/60 is non-terminating because:
mcqs.why: 23/60 is in lowest form and 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. Even though 2 and 5 are present, the extra prime 3 makes it non-terminating: 23/60 = 0.38333… One other prime is enough.

lessons.title: Exercise 3.4 — Fractions and Mixed Numbers as Decimals
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

This exercise mixes three skills: plain fractions, mixed numbers, and fractions that must be simplified first. For every number you find the decimal and say if it is terminating or non-terminating recurring.

For a mixed number, first change it to an improper fraction. For example −3 21/22 = −87/22. Then divide.

Formula / Rule

Mixed number to improper fraction: multiply the whole part by the denominator, add the numerator, and keep the same denominator. Then divide numerator by denominator to get the decimal.

Simplify first when you can: 91/65 = 7/5, −153/85 = −9/5, 272/288 = 17/18 — the decimal is much easier after simplifying.

Worked Example

Convert 3 27/32 into a decimal.

Step 1: Change to an improper fraction: 3 × 32 + 27 = 123, so 3 27/32 = 123/32.

Step 2: Divide: 123 ÷ 32 = 3.84375.

Step 3: The division ends, remainder 0.

Step 4: Answer: 3 27/32 = 3.84375, a terminating decimal.

More Types in This Exercise

  • Recurring plain fractions: 5/14 = 0.357142… (group 571428), −13/18 = −0.7222… (2 repeats).
  • Terminating plain fractions: 19/20 = 0.95, 23/40 = 0.575.
  • Recurring mixed numbers: −3 21/22 = −3.954545… (group 54), 6 17/30 = 6.5666… (6 repeats).
  • Terminating mixed numbers: −3 49/50 = −3.98, 2 45/48 = 47/16 = 2.9375.
  • Simplify-first fractions: 266/171 = 14/9 = 1.555… recurring, 272/288 = 17/18 = 0.9444… recurring.

Remember

  • Always convert mixed numbers before dividing.
  • Keep the minus sign through every step.
  • Simplifying first can turn a hard division into an easy one, like 91/65 = 7/5 = 1.4.

mcqs.q: 5/14 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: 5 ÷ 14 = 0.357142857142… where the group 571428 repeats. So it is non-terminating recurring. The decimal never reaches remainder 0.

mcqs.q: −13/18 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: −13 ÷ 18 = −0.7222… where the digit 2 repeats forever. So it is non-terminating recurring and negative. The minus sign must stay in the answer.

mcqs.q: 19/20 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: 19 ÷ 20 = 0.95 and the division ends exactly. So 19/20 is a terminating decimal. This same fraction appears in Exercise 3.2 with the same result.

mcqs.q: −3 21/22 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: First −3 21/22 = −87/22. Then −87 ÷ 22 = −3.954545… where group 54 repeats. So it is non-terminating recurring. Mixed numbers must be changed to improper fractions first.

mcqs.q: 23/40 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: 23 ÷ 40 = 0.575 and the division ends. So 23/40 is terminating. Denominator 40 has only primes 2 and 5 after considering lowest form, which fits the rule.

mcqs.q: 3 27/32 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: 3 27/32 = 123/32, and 123 ÷ 32 = 3.84375 exactly. The division ends, so it is terminating. This is the clearest mixed-number terminating example in the exercise.

mcqs.q: −3 49/50 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: −3 49/50 = −199/50, and −199 ÷ 50 = −3.98 exactly. So it is terminating and negative. Denominator 50 gives a short decimal.

mcqs.q: 91/65 simplifies to 7/5, so as a decimal it is:
mcqs.why: 91/65 = 7/5 after dividing top and bottom by 13. Then 7 ÷ 5 = 1.4, which ends. Simplifying first makes this question very easy.

mcqs.q: 266/171 simplifies to 14/9, so as a decimal it is:
mcqs.why: 266/171 = 14/9, and 14 ÷ 9 = 1.555… where 5 repeats. So it is non-terminating recurring. Always simplify before you judge the type.

mcqs.q: 2 45/48 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: 2 45/48 = 141/48 = 47/16, and 47 ÷ 16 = 2.9375 exactly. So it is terminating. Simplifying the mixed number to 47/16 is the key step.

lessons.title: Exercise 3.5 — Converting and Rounding to 2 and 3 Decimal Places
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

This is the biggest rounding exercise. You convert fractions to decimals, say if they are terminating or non-terminating, and then round the answer to 3 decimal places (Part I), to 2 decimal places (Part II), or round decimals that are already given (Parts IV and V).

Formula / Rule

Rounding rule: to round to 2 decimal places, look at the 3rd digit. To round to 3 decimal places, look at the 4th digit. If that digit is 5 or more, increase the last kept digit by 1; otherwise it stays the same.

Watch the carry case: 3.9995 to 2 decimal places becomes 4.00, because 9 + 1 = 10 and the extra 1 carries forward.

Worked Example

Convert 23/400 into a decimal and round it to 3 decimal places.

Step 1: Divide: 23 ÷ 400 = 0.0575.

Step 2: The decimal ends, so it is terminating.

Step 3: To round to 3 decimal places, look at the 4th digit, which is 5.

Step 4: 5 means round up, so the 3rd digit 7 becomes 8.

Step 5: Answer: 0.058 to 3 decimal places.

More Types in This Exercise

  • Terminating then round: 27/64 = 0.421875 → 0.422 to 3 dp; 77/80 = 0.9625 → 0.963 to 3 dp; 246/300 = 0.82 → 0.820 to 3 dp.
  • Non-terminating then round: 53/60 = 0.88333… → 0.883 to 3 dp; 69/70 = 0.985714… → 0.986 to 3 dp.
  • Round to 2 dp: 4/15 = 0.2666… → 0.27; 22/7 = 3.142857… → 3.14; 3/40 = 0.075 → 0.08.
  • Recurring to 3 dp: 10/11 = 0.9090… → 0.909; 9/7 = 1.285714… → 1.286; 17/19 = 0.894736… → 0.895.
  • Given decimals: 0.4555 → 0.46 to 2 dp, 0.3648 → 0.36 to 2 dp, 4.51689 → 4.517 to 3 dp, 0.0098 → 0.010 to 3 dp.

Remember

  • Say the type AND give the rounded value — both are asked.
  • Keep trailing zeros in rounded answers: 0.820, −0.40 and 4.00 are correct forms.
  • For negative numbers, round the digits the same way and keep the minus sign.

mcqs.q: 23/400 = 0.0575 rounded to 3 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: 23/400 = 0.0575 is terminating. For 3 decimal places look at the 4th digit, which is 5, so round up: 7 becomes 8. The rounded value is 0.058.

mcqs.q: 27/64 = 0.421875 rounded to 3 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: 27/64 = 0.421875 is terminating. The 4th digit is 8, which is 5 or more, so the 3rd digit 1 increases to 2. The answer to 3 dp is 0.422.

mcqs.q: 53/60 = 0.88333… rounded to 3 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: 53/60 is non-terminating: 0.88333… The 4th digit is 3, which is less than 5, so the 3rd digit stays the same. Rounded to 3 dp it is 0.883.

mcqs.q: 77/80 = 0.9625 rounded to 3 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: 77/80 = 0.9625 is terminating. The 4th digit is 5, so round up: the 3rd digit 2 becomes 3. To 3 decimal places the answer is 0.963.

mcqs.q: 4/15 = 0.2666… rounded to 2 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: 4/15 is non-terminating: 0.2666… For 2 decimal places look at the 3rd digit, which is 6, so round up. The answer is 0.27.

mcqs.q: 22/7 = 3.142857… rounded to 2 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: 22/7 = 3.142857… is non-terminating. The 3rd digit is 2, less than 5, so the 2nd digit stays the same. Rounded to 2 dp it is 3.14, the famous approximation for pi in this book.

mcqs.q: 3/40 = 0.075 rounded to 2 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: 3/40 = 0.075 is terminating. For 2 decimal places look at the 3rd digit, which is 5, so round up: 7 becomes 8. The answer is 0.08.

mcqs.q: 10/11 = 0.9090… rounded to 3 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: 10/11 is non-terminating recurring with group 90: 0.9090… The 4th digit is 0, so the 3rd digit stays the same. To 3 dp the answer is 0.909.

mcqs.q: 9/7 = 1.285714… rounded to 3 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: 9/7 = 1.285714… is non-terminating recurring. The 4th digit is 7, which is 5 or more, so the 3rd digit 5 increases to 6. The answer is 1.286.

mcqs.q: 0.4555 rounded to 2 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: For 2 decimal places look at the 3rd digit, which is 5. The rule says 5 or more means round up, so 5 becomes 6. 0.4555 → 0.46.

mcqs.q: 0.3648 rounded to 2 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: For 2 decimal places look at the 3rd digit, which is 4. Since 4 is less than 5, the 2nd digit stays the same. 0.3648 → 0.36.

mcqs.q: 3.9995 rounded to 2 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: The 3rd digit is 9, so the 2nd digit 9 increases by 1: 9 + 1 = 10, so you carry. This gives 4.00. This is the special carry case in Part IV — do not write 3.910 or 3.99.

mcqs.q: 4.51689 rounded to 3 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: For 3 decimal places look at the 4th digit, which is 8. Since 8 is 5 or more, the 3rd digit 6 increases to 7. 4.51689 → 4.517.

mcqs.q: 0.0098 rounded to 3 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: For 3 decimal places look at the 4th digit, which is 8, so round up: the 3rd digit 9 becomes 10, giving a carry. 0.0098 → 0.010. Keep all 3 decimal places in the answer.

mcqs.q: 59.9196 rounded to 3 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: For 3 decimal places look at the 4th digit, which is 6, so round up: the 3rd digit 9 increases and carries within the decimal part. 59.9196 → 59.920. The final 0 must be written.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 3 — Decimal Fractions: Mixed Practice
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

The Review mixes everything in Unit 3: decimals to fractions, fractions to decimals, splitting terminating from non-terminating, and rounding to 2 and 3 decimal places. It also asks the theory: definitions, the 2-and-5 rule, and what rounding means.

The two parts of a decimal are the whole part and the decimal part, separated by the decimal point (.). For example in 3.5, 3 is the whole part and 5 is in the decimal part.

Formula / Rule

Terminating test: in lowest form, if the denominator has only prime factors 2 and/or 5, the decimal terminates; otherwise it is non-terminating.

Rounding: if the next digit is 5 or more, increase the last kept digit by 1; otherwise it stays the same. A recurring decimal is a non-terminating decimal where a digit or a group of digits repeats, like 0.333… or 0.142857…

Worked Example

Convert 0.325 into a rational number in lowest form.

Step 1: 0.325 has 3 decimal places, so write 0.325 = 325/1000.

Step 2: Divide 325 and 1000 by 25.

Step 3: 325 ÷ 25 = 13 and 1000 ÷ 25 = 40.

Step 4: Answer: 0.325 = 13/40.

More Types in This Review

  • Decimals to fractions: 0.75 = 3/4, 2.5 = 5/2, 7.75 = 31/4, 0.52 = 13/25, 1.4375 = 23/16.
  • Fractions to decimals: 41/5 = 8.2 terminating, 21/16 = 1.3125 terminating, 28/9 = 3.111… recurring, 22/7 = 3.142857… recurring.
  • Splitting: 13/4 = 3.25 and 17/25 = 0.68 are terminating; 80/3 = 26.666…, 15/11 = 1.3636… and 19/6 = 3.1666… are non-terminating.
  • Rounding: 14.5828 → 14.58 to 2 dp, 5.71679 → 5.717 to 3 dp, 40/3 = 13.333… → 13.333 to 3 dp, 80/13 → 6.154 to 3 dp.

Remember

  • In a terminating decimal the division ends after a limited number of steps.
  • In a recurring decimal a digit or group of digits comes again and again.
  • For recurring decimals the book also shows the 9s method: 0.333… = 3/9 = 1/3.

mcqs.q: 0.325 in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 0.325 = 325/1000 because there are 3 decimal places. Dividing by 25 gives 13/40. This is Question 1 of the Review and follows the Exercise 3.1 method exactly.

mcqs.q: 0.75 in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 0.75 = 75/100, and dividing by 25 gives 3/4. The Review asks this twice — in Question 1 and in the objective Question 10 — with the same answer 3/4.

mcqs.q: 2.5 in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 2.5 = 25/10 with 1 decimal place. Dividing by 5 gives 5/2. Numbers greater than 1 give improper fractions in lowest form.

mcqs.q: 7.75 in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 7.75 = 775/100 with 2 decimal places. Dividing by 25 gives 31/4. Always simplify fully — 775/100 is not lowest form.

mcqs.q: 41/5 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: 41 ÷ 5 = 8.2 and the division ends exactly. So 41/5 is a terminating decimal. Denominator 5 fits the only-2-and-5 rule for terminating decimals.

mcqs.q: 28/9 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: 28 ÷ 9 = 3.111… where the digit 1 repeats forever. So it is non-terminating recurring. Denominator 9 has prime factor 3, so it cannot terminate.

mcqs.q: 21/16 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: 21 ÷ 16 = 1.3125 and the division ends. So it is terminating. Denominator 16 is only 2s (2 × 2 × 2 × 2), which is why it terminates.

mcqs.q: 14.5828 rounded to 2 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: For 2 decimal places look at the 3rd digit, which is 2. Since 2 is less than 5, the 2nd digit stays the same. 14.5828 → 14.58.

mcqs.q: 107.8287 rounded to 2 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: For 2 decimal places look at the 3rd digit, which is 8, so round up: 2 becomes 3. 107.8287 → 107.83. The book prints this number without its decimal point, but it is read as 107.8287.

mcqs.q: Which pair is correct?
mcqs.why: 13 ÷ 4 = 3.25 ends, so 13/4 is terminating. 80 ÷ 3 = 26.666… never ends, so 80/3 is non-terminating. Question 4 of the Review asks you to split fractions exactly like this.

mcqs.q: 0.52 in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 0.52 = 52/100 with 2 decimal places. Dividing by 4 gives 13/25. 13 and 25 have no common divisor, so this is lowest form.

mcqs.q: 1.4375 in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 1.4375 = 14375/10000 with 4 decimal places. Dividing by 625 gives 23/16. This is one of the harder conversions in Question 5 of the Review.

mcqs.q: 40/3 = 13.333… rounded to 3 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: 40/3 = 13.333… is non-terminating recurring. The 4th digit is 3, less than 5, so the 3rd digit stays the same. To 3 dp it is 13.333.

mcqs.q: 5.71679 rounded to 3 decimal places is:
mcqs.why: For 3 decimal places look at the 4th digit, which is 7, so round up: 6 becomes 7. 5.71679 → 5.717. This is Question 7 of the Review.

mcqs.q: A rational number is terminating if the prime factors of its denominator (in lowest form) are only:
mcqs.why: The rule from Question 8 and Question 10 is: only 2 and/or 5 in the denominator means terminating. Any other prime, like 3 or 7, means non-terminating. The whole part and decimal part are separated by the point (.) in the same theory section.

lessons.title: Exercise 4.1 — Powers: Base and Exponent
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

A power is a short way to write the same number multiplied many times. For example, 2^5 means 2 multiplied by itself 5 times.

The number that is multiplied is called the base. The small number written at the top is called the exponent. The exponent tells us how many times to multiply the base.

Formula / Rule

a^n = a × a × a × ... (n times)

If the base is negative and the exponent is odd, the answer is negative. If the exponent is even, the answer is positive.

Worked Example

Find the value of 2^7.

Step 1: Write it in expanded form: 2^7 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2.

Step 2: Multiply step by step: 2 × 2 = 4, 4 × 2 = 8, 8 × 2 = 16, 16 × 2 = 32, 32 × 2 = 64, 64 × 2 = 128.

Step 3: So 2^7 = 128.

Another example from the exercise: 2³ × 3⁴ = (2 × 2 × 2) × (3 × 3 × 3 × 3) = 8 × 81 = 648.

Writing a Number in Exponential Form

To write a number as a power, break it into equal factors. For example, 1000 = 10 × 10 × 10 = 10³, and 512 = 2 multiplied 9 times = 2^9.

For a fraction, write the top and bottom separately: 32/243 = (2/3)^5 because 32 = 2^5 and 243 = 3^5.

Remember

  • Base = the number being multiplied. Exponent = how many times it is multiplied.
  • Negative base with an odd exponent gives a negative answer, e.g. (−3)³ = −27.
  • Negative base with an even exponent gives a positive answer, e.g. (−1/4)⁴ = 1/256.
  • Examples to know: 3² = 9, 5⁴ = 625, 6³ = 216, 625 = 5⁴, −343 = (−7)³.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 3²?
mcqs.why: 3² means 3 × 3. Multiplying gives 9. The exponent 2 tells us to multiply the base 3 two times, not to multiply 3 by 2.

mcqs.q: In 2^5, what are the base and the exponent?
mcqs.why: The base is the number being multiplied, which is 2. The exponent is the small number at the top, which is 5. So 2^5 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 2^7?
mcqs.why: 2^7 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2. Multiplying step by step gives 128. This is the expanded form given in the exercise.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 5⁴?
What is (−3)³?
mcqs.why: (−3)³ = (−3) × (−3) × (−3) = 9 × (−3) = −27. The exponent 3 is odd, so a negative base gives a negative answer.

mcqs.q: What is (−1/4)⁴?
mcqs.why: (−1/4)⁴ means −1/4 multiplied by itself 4 times. The exponent 4 is even, so the answer is positive: 1/256. Even exponents remove the minus sign.

mcqs.q: Which exponential form is equal to 1000?
mcqs.why: 1000 = 10 × 10 × 10, which is 10 multiplied 3 times. So 1000 = 10³. Counting the equal factors gives the exponent.

mcqs.q: 512 written in exponential form is:
mcqs.why: 512 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2, which is nine 2s multiplied together. So 512 = 2^9.

mcqs.q: What is 2³ × 3⁴?
mcqs.why: 2³ = 8 and 3⁴ = 81. Then 8 × 81 = 648. Work out each power first, then multiply the values.

mcqs.q: 32/243 in exponential form is:
mcqs.why: 32 = 2^5 and 243 = 3^5, so both parts have exponent 5. Therefore 32/243 = (2/3)^5. Write the numerator and denominator as powers first.

lessons.title: Exercise 4.2 — Product Law of Exponents
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

This exercise is about multiplying powers. There are two easy cases: same base, and same exponent.

Formula / Rule

Product law (same base): a^m × a^n = a^(m+n) — add the exponents.

Same exponent: a^n × b^n = (a × b)^n — multiply the bases, keep the exponent.

Worked Example

Simplify (5/7)² × (5/7)⁴.

Step 1: The base 5/7 is the same in both powers.

Step 2: Add the exponents: 2 + 4 = 6.

Step 3: So (5/7)² × (5/7)⁴ = (5/7)^6.

Another example: (3/4)^6 × (1/5)^6 = (3/4 × 1/5)^6 = (3/20)^6, because the exponent 6 is the same.

More Types in This Exercise

With letters the same rules work: p^6 × p^7 = p^13, and x^5 × y^5 × z^5 = (xyz)^5.

Collect like bases first: y^5 × x^11 × y^6 = x^11 × y^11 = (xy)^11, because y^5 × y^6 = y^11.

Remember

  • Same base when multiplying: ADD the exponents, do not multiply them.
  • Same exponent when multiplying: MULTIPLY the bases.
  • Check example: 2^5 × 3^5 = 6^5, and (3/4)⁴ × (3/4)^8 = (3/4)^12.
  • An even final exponent makes a negative base positive, e.g. (−5/7)^16 = (5/7)^16.

mcqs.why: The base 5/7 is the same, so we add the exponents: 2 + 4 = 6. This gives (5/7)^6. This is the product law for the same base.
The exponent 6 is the same, so we multiply the bases: 3/4 × 1/5 = 3/20. The answer is (3/20)^6. Keep the exponent the same in this case.
Both powers have the same base p, so add the exponents: 6 + 7 = 13. So p^6 × p^7 = p^13. Do not multiply 6 × 7 here.
All three powers have the same base 4/3, so add all the exponents: 5 + 6 + 7 = 18. The result is (4/3)^18.
All three powers have the same exponent 5, so multiply the bases together: x × y × z = xyz. The answer is (xyz)^5.

mcqs.q: y^5 × x^11 × y^6 simplifies to:
mcqs.why: First collect the y powers: y^5 × y^6 = y^11. So we get x^11 × y^11, which can also be written as (xy)^11. Always group the same bases first.
Add the exponents: 6 + 5 + 3 = 14, giving (−1/3)^14. Since 14 is even, this equals (1/3)^14, a positive value.

mcqs.q: Which check is correct?
mcqs.why: With the same exponent 5, multiply the bases: 2 × 3 = 6. So 2^5 × 3^5 = (2 × 3)^5 = 6^5, as checked in the exercise.
The base is the same, so add the exponents: 4 + 8 = 12. The result is (3/4)^12, exactly as in the checking question.

mcqs.q: p² × q^7 × p^5 simplifies to:
mcqs.why: Collect the p powers: p² × p^5 = p^7. Then p^7 × q^7 has the same exponent 7, so it equals (pq)^7. Use both product rules in one question.

lessons.title: Exercise 4.3 — Division Law of Exponents
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

This exercise is about dividing powers. Like multiplication, there are two easy cases: same base, and same exponent.

Formula / Rule

Division law (same base): a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m−n) — subtract the exponents.

Same exponent: a^n ÷ b^n = (a ÷ b)^n — divide the bases, keep the exponent.

Worked Example

Simplify 5^7 ÷ 5⁴.

Step 1: The base 5 is the same.

Step 2: Subtract the exponents: 7 − 4 = 3.

Step 3: So 5^7 ÷ 5⁴ = 5³ = 125.

Another example: (10)^5 ÷ (2)^5 = (10/2)^5 = 5^5 = 3125, because the exponent 5 is the same.

More Types in This Exercise

With fractions: (5/7)^5 ÷ (5/7)² = (5/7)³ = 125/343, and (2/5)^6 ÷ (3/5)^6 = (2/3)^6 = 64/729.

If the exponents become 1, the answer is just the base: (7/11)^6 ÷ (7/11)^5 = (7/11)^1 = 7/11.

Remember
