Each term contains a, b and c once in common: abc.
Divide each term by abc to get a, b, c.
Result: abc(a + b + c).

mcqs.q: Factorise: 13n − 2n³ + 39n⁵ = ?
mcqs.why:
Common factor is n (lowest power is n¹).
13n÷n=13, −2n³÷n=−2n², 39n⁵÷n=39n⁴.
Result: n(13 − 2n² + 39n⁴).

mcqs.q: Factorise: 3a(b + c) + 6d(b + c) = ?
mcqs.why:
The bracket (b + c) is common, giving (b + c)(3a + 6d).
Then 3a + 6d still has factor 3: 3(a + 2d).
Full answer: 3(b + c)(a + 2d).

mcqs.q: The common factor in pq(p² − q)² + pr(p² − q)² + qr(p² − q)² is:
mcqs.why:
Every part contains the bracket (p² − q)².
So that whole bracket is the common factor.
Factorised form: (p² − q)²(pq + pr + qr).

mcqs.q: Factorise: 4lm(x − y) + 8mn(x − y)² + 12nl(x − y). The first factor taken out is:
mcqs.why:
Numbers 4, 8, 12 have HCF 4, and (x − y) is in every part.
So take out 4(x − y) first.
Inside remains lm + 2mn(x − y) + 3nl.

mcqs.q: To check a factorisation, you should:
options: Expand it back — it must give the original
mcqs.why:
Factorising is the reverse of expanding.
If you expand your answer, you must get the original expression.
This is the safest way to check.

lessons.title: Exercise 8.9 — Factorising Perfect Squares
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

Some trinomials are perfect squares: they came from (a + b)² or (a − b)². The first and last terms are squares, and the middle term is twice the product of their square roots.

Formula / Rule

a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)²

a² − 2ab + b² = (a − b)²

Worked Example

Factorise x² + 12x + 36.

Step 1: First term is square of x.

Step 2: Last term 36 is square of 6.

Step 3: Check middle: 2 × x × 6 = 12x. It matches.

Step 4: So x² + 12x + 36 = (x + 6)².

With a Common Factor First

4a² + 48a + 144: take out 4 first → 4(a² + 12a + 36) = 4(a + 6)².

3s² − 48st + 192t² = 3(s − 8t)².

The sign of the middle term tells + or − inside: negative middle means (a − b)².

Remember

  • Always check the middle term equals 2 × root1 × root2.
  • Take out any common factor before checking for a perfect square.
  • (2a + 3)² comes from 4a² + 12a + 9.

mcqs.q: Factorise: x² + 12x + 36 = ?
mcqs.why:
√(x²) = x and √36 = 6. Middle check: 2 × x × 6 = 12x ✓.
So it is a perfect square: (x + 6)².
The middle term is positive, so use +.

mcqs.q: Factorise: a² + 4a + 4 = ?
mcqs.why:
√4 = 2, and 2 × a × 2 = 4a matches the middle term.
So a² + 4a + 4 = (a + 2)².
Always verify with the middle term.

mcqs.q: Factorise: 4a² + 12a + 9 = ?
mcqs.why:
√(4a²) = 2a and √9 = 3.
Middle: 2 × 2a × 3 = 12a ✓.
Result: (2a + 3)².

mcqs.q: Factorise: 9x² + 42xy + 49y² = ?
mcqs.why:
Roots are 3x and 7y.
Middle: 2 × 3x × 7y = 42xy ✓.
Result: (3x + 7y)².

mcqs.q: Factorise: 16b² + 40b + 25 = ?
Factorise: 4a² + 48a + 144 = ?
mcqs.why:
First take out common factor 4: 4(a² + 12a + 36).
Inside is (x + 6) pattern with a: (a + 6)².
Full answer: 4(a + 6)².

mcqs.q: Factorise: 5y² + 40y + 80 = ?
mcqs.why:
Take out 5: 5(y² + 8y + 16).
Inside: √16 = 4 and 2 × y × 4 = 8y ✓, so (y + 4)².
Answer: 5(y + 4)².

mcqs.q: Factorise: 3s² − 48st + 192t² = ?
mcqs.why:
Take out 3: 3(s² − 16st + 64t²).
Inside roots s and 8t, middle −2×s×8t = −16st ✓.
Negative middle means minus: 3(s − 8t)².

mcqs.q: Factorise: 4a⁴ − 12a² + 9 = ?
mcqs.why:
√(4a⁴) = 2a² and √9 = 3.
Middle: 2 × 2a² × 3 = 12a², with minus sign ✓.
Result: (2a² − 3)².

mcqs.q: In a perfect-square trinomial, the middle term must equal:
mcqs.why:
A perfect square a² ± 2ab + b² has middle term 2ab.
That is 2 × root of first × root of last.
If the middle does not match, it is not a perfect square.

lessons.title: Exercise 8.10 — Factorising Difference of Two Squares
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

A difference of two squares has two square terms joined by minus. It factorises into (root1 + root2)(root1 − root2).

Formula / Rule

a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b)

Worked Example

Factorise 4x² − 9.

Step 1: 4x² is the square of 2x.

Step 2: 9 is the square of 3.

Step 3: Write (2x + 3)(2x − 3).

Harder Cases

Take out a common factor first if needed: 6x² − 24 = 6(x + 2)(x − 2).

Squares can be brackets: (2x + 3y)² − 100z² = (2x + 3y + 10z)(2x + 3y − 10z).

36 − (3a − 2b)² = (6 + 3a − 2b)(6 − 3a + 2b).

Remember

  • It must be a minus between two squares — a sum of squares does not factorise this way.
  • One bracket gets +, the other gets −.
  • Find square roots carefully: √(81a²) = 9a, √(121b²) = 11b.

mcqs.q: Factorise: b² − c² = ?
mcqs.why:
b² − c² is a difference of two squares.
a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b), so the answer is (b + c)(b − c).
One bracket has +, one has −.

mcqs.q: Factorise: a² − 36 = ?
mcqs.why:
36 = 6², so a² − 36 = a² − 6².
Using a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b) gives (a + 6)(a − 6).
Find the square root of 36 first.

mcqs.q: Factorise: 25 − y² = ?
mcqs.why:
25 = 5², so 25 − y² = 5² − y².
It factorises as (5 + y)(5 − y).
Order does not matter — roots are 5 and y.

mcqs.q: Factorise: 4x² − 9 = ?
mcqs.why:
√(4x²) = 2x and √9 = 3.
So 4x² − 9 = (2x + 3)(2x − 3).
Square the coefficient too: √4 = 2.

mcqs.q: Factorise: 9x² − 16y² = ?
mcqs.why:
√(9x²) = 3x and √(16y²) = 4y.
Difference of squares gives (3x + 4y)(3x − 4y).
Each root keeps its letter.

mcqs.q: Factorise: 6x² − 24 = ?
mcqs.why:
First take out 6: 6(x² − 4).
Then x² − 4 = (x + 2)(x − 2).
Full answer: 6(x + 2)(x − 2). Do not stop at the first step.

mcqs.q: Factorise: 81a² − 121b² = ?
mcqs.why:
√(81a²) = 9a and √(121b²) = 11b (since 11² = 121).
So the factors are (9a + 11b)(9a − 11b).
Know your squares: 11² = 121.

mcqs.q: Factorise: (2x + 3y)² − 100z² = ?
mcqs.why:
Treat (2x + 3y) as one root and √(100z²) = 10z as the other.
Difference of squares: (2x + 3y + 10z)(2x + 3y − 10z).
A whole bracket can be a 'square root' here.

mcqs.q: Factorise: 200 − 18z² = ?
mcqs.why:
Take out 2: 2(100 − 9z²).
100 = 10² and 9z² = (3z)², so inside = (10 + 3z)(10 − 3z).
Full answer: 2(10 + 3z)(10 − 3z).

mcqs.q: 64b² − (6b + d)² factorises as:
mcqs.why:
Roots are 8b and (6b + d).
Sum bracket: 8b + 6b + d = 14b + d. Difference: 8b − 6b − d = 2b − d.
Result: (14b + d)(2b − d).

lessons.title: Exercise 8.11 — Factorising by Grouping and Splitting the Middle Term
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

For trinomials like x² + bx + c, split the middle term into two parts whose sum is b and whose product is c. Then group in pairs and take out common factors. The same grouping idea works for four-term expressions.

Formula / Rule

x² + (p + q)x + pq = (x + p)(x + q), where p + q = middle coefficient and p × q = constant.

Worked Example

Factorise x² + 6x + 8.

Step 1: Find two numbers with sum 6 and product 8: 2 and 4.

Step 2: Split: x² + 2x + 4x + 8.

Step 3: Group: x(x + 2) + 4(x + 2).

Step 4: Answer = (x + 2)(x + 4).

Sign Rules

If c is positive, both numbers have the same sign as b. If c is negative, the numbers have opposite signs.

Grouping example: ax + ay + bx + by = a(x + y) + b(x + y) = (x + y)(a + b).

Some trinomials like m² − 5m + 14 cannot be factorised with whole numbers — say so honestly.

Remember

  • Always check: sum = middle coefficient, product = constant × x² coefficient.
  • Take out a common factor first if there is one.
  • The bracket left in both groups must be identical.

mcqs.q: Factorise by grouping: ax + ay + bx + by = ?
mcqs.why:
Group: a(x + y) + b(x + y).
The common bracket (x + y) comes out.
Result: (x + y)(a + b).

mcqs.q: Factorise: x² + 6x + 8 = ?
mcqs.why:
Need sum 6, product 8: numbers 2 and 4.
Split: x² + 2x + 4x + 8 = x(x + 2) + 4(x + 2).
Result: (x + 2)(x + 4).

mcqs.q: Factorise: y² + 8y + 12 = ?
mcqs.why:
Sum 8, product 12: 2 and 6 (3 and 4 give product 12 but sum 7).
So y² + 8y + 12 = (y + 2)(y + 6).
Both sum and product must match.

mcqs.q: Factorise: c² + 5c + 6 = ?
mcqs.why:
Sum 5, product 6: numbers 2 and 3.
Split and group to get (c + 2)(c + 3).
Check: 2 + 3 = 5 and 2 × 3 = 6 ✓.

mcqs.q: Factorise: p² − 4p + 3 = ?
mcqs.why:
Sum −4, product +3: numbers −1 and −3.
Both negative because sum is negative and product positive.
Result: (p − 1)(p − 3).

mcqs.q: Factorise: a² + 3a − 10 = ?
mcqs.why:
Product −10 means opposite signs. Sum +3: numbers +5 and −2.
So a² + 3a − 10 = (a + 5)(a − 2).
5 + (−2) = 3 and 5 × (−2) = −10 ✓.

mcqs.q: Factorise: x² − 2x − 15 = ?
mcqs.why:
Product −15, sum −2: numbers −5 and +3.
Split: x² − 5x + 3x − 15 = x(x − 5) + 3(x − 5).
Result: (x − 5)(x + 3).

mcqs.q: Factorise: y² + 7y − 18 = ?
mcqs.why:
Product −18, sum +7: numbers +9 and −2.
9 + (−2) = 7 and 9 × (−2) = −18 ✓.
Result: (y + 9)(y − 2).

mcqs.q: Factorise: 5x² + 9x + 4 = ?
mcqs.why:
Split 9x as 5x + 4x: 5x² + 5x + 4x + 4.
Group: 5x(x + 1) + 4(x + 1) = (x + 1)(5x + 4).
Grouping works even when x² has a coefficient.

We need two integers with sum −5 and product 14 — none exist.
The discriminant 25 − 56 = −31 is negative.
So m² − 5m + 14 has no integer factors. Not every trinomial factorises.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 8 — Algebraic Expressions: Mixed Practice
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

This review mixes everything in Unit 8: definitions, the three identities, adding and subtracting expressions like A, B, C, simplifying products, proving identities, and all factorisation methods.

Formula / Rule

(a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²

(a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²

(a + b)(a − b) = a² − b²

(x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab

Worked Example

For A = 2(x² + y² + z²), B = −x² + 3y² + 2z², C = x² − y² − 3z², find A + B + C.

Step 1: A = 2x² + 2y² + 2z².

Step 2: Add x² terms: 2 − 1 + 1 = 2, so 2x².

Step 3: Add y² terms: 2 + 3 − 1 = 4, so 4y².

Step 4: Add z² terms: 2 + 2 − 3 = 1, so z².

Step 5: A + B + C = 2x² + 4y² + z².

Key Definitions

  • Numerical coefficient: the fixed number multiplying a variable, e.g. 5 in 5x.
  • Constant: a symbol with a fixed value, e.g. 3, −5.
  • Binomial: an expression with two terms, e.g. 2x + 5.
  • Factorisation: writing an expression as a product of factors.
  • Literal numbers: symbols used for numerical values. Monomial: one term only.

Remember

  • When subtracting A, B or C, flip every sign.
  • Simplify (x − 2y)(x + 2y) = x² − 4y² with difference of squares.
  • Factorise in order: common factor first, then perfect square or difference of squares.

mcqs.q: In 5x, the number 5 is called the:
mcqs.why:
In 5x, x is the variable and 5 is the fixed number multiplying it.
That fixed number is the numerical coefficient.
The book's MCQ also accepts it as the constant part of the term.

mcqs.q: A constant is:
options: A symbol with a fixed numerical value, e.g. 3, −5
mcqs.why:
A constant never changes its value: 3 is always 3, −5 is always −5.
Letters like x are variables because their value can change.
So a constant is a fixed numerical value.

mcqs.q: 3x + 5 is what kind of expression?
mcqs.why:
3x + 5 has two terms: 3x and 5.
An expression with two terms is a binomial.
One term would be a monomial; three would be a trinomial.

mcqs.q: The factors of x² − x are:
mcqs.why:
Take out the common factor x: x² − x = x(x − 1).
Check by expanding: x(x − 1) = x² − x ✓.
Option (a) would give x² + x, which is wrong.

mcqs.q: The factors of a² − 9 are:
mcqs.why:
a² − 9 = a² − 3², a difference of two squares.
So it factorises as (a + 3)(a − 3).
Use √(9) = 3, not 9 itself.

mcqs.q: (x − y)² equals:
mcqs.why:
Use (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² with a = x, b = y.
That gives x² − 2xy + y².
The last term is +y², never −y².

The square of a sum identity is (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b².
All three terms are positive.
This is one of the fill-in-the-blank identities in the review.

A difference of two squares factorises as (a + b)(a − b).
Expanding the right side gives a² − b² because the middle terms cancel.
This is the reverse of the product identity.

mcqs.q: For A = 2x² + 2y² + 2z², B = −x² + 3y² + 2z², C = x² − y² − 3z²: A + B + C = ?
mcqs.why:
Add letter by letter: x²: 2 − 1 + 1 = 2. y²: 2 + 3 − 1 = 4.
z²: 2 + 2 − 3 = 1.
So A + B + C = 2x² + 4y² + z².

mcqs.q: With the same A, B, C: A + B − C = ?
mcqs.why:
Subtracting C flips its signs: −x² + y² + 3z² is added.
x²: 2 − 1 − 1 = 0. y²: 2 + 3 + 1 = 6. z²: 2 + 2 + 3 = 7.
Result: 6y² + 7z² (the x² terms cancel).

mcqs.q: Simplify: (x − 2y)(x + 2y) = ?
mcqs.why:
This is (a − b)(a + b) = a² − b² with a = x, b = 2y.
(2y)² = 4y², so the result is x² − 4y².
Square the whole 2y term.

mcqs.q: Simplify: (4x²)(3x + 1) = ?
mcqs.why:
Multiply both terms by 4x²: 4x² × 3x = 12x³.
4x² × 1 = 4x².
Result: 12x³ + 4x².

mcqs.q: Prove-type: (3x − 5)(3x + 5) = ?
mcqs.why:
Use difference of squares: (3x)² − 5².
(3x)² = 9x² and 5² = 25.
So the product is 9x² − 25, with no middle term.

mcqs.q: Factorise: 10a² − 200a⁴b = ?
mcqs.why:
The HCF of both terms is 10a².
10a² ÷ 10a² = 1 and −200a⁴b ÷ 10a² = −20a²b.
Result: 10a²(1 − 20a²b).

mcqs.q: Factorise: a² − 26a + 169 = ?
mcqs.why:
169 = 13² and 2 × a × 13 = 26a matches the middle term.
The middle is negative, so use minus.
Result: (a − 13)², a perfect square.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.1 — Solving Linear Equations
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

A linear equation has one variable with power 1, like x. To solve it, do the same thing to both sides until x is alone. Whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other side too.

This exercise has four kinds of questions: simple equations, equations with brackets, equations where x² terms cancel, and equations with fractions where you cross-multiply or multiply by the LCM.

Formula / Rule

Add or subtract the same number on both sides to move numbers.

Multiply or divide both sides by the same number to free x.

For fractions: multiply both sides by the LCM, or cross-multiply.

Worked Example

Solve: 9 + 5x = 3x + 13.

Step 1: Subtract 3x from both sides: 9 + 2x = 13.

Step 2: Subtract 9 from both sides: 2x = 4.

Step 3: Divide both sides by 2: x = 2.

Remember

  • Open brackets first. Example: 5 + 3(x − 1) = 5x − 6 becomes 3x + 2 = 5x − 6, giving x = 4.
  • In (x + 2)(x + 3) = (x − 3)(x − 2) + 20, the x² terms cancel and 10x = 20, so x = 2.
  • For 8 ÷ x = 2, multiply both sides by x: 8 = 2x, so x = 4.

mcqs.q: Solve: x + 5 = 9. What is x?
mcqs.why: Subtract 5 from both sides: x + 5 − 5 = 9 − 5, so x = 4. Do the opposite operation to move the 5 to the other side.

mcqs.q: Solve: 12 − x = 7. What is x?
mcqs.why: Subtract 12 from both sides: −x = 7 − 12 = −5, so x = 5. When −x equals −5, x itself equals 5.

mcqs.q: Solve: 5x = 3. What is x?
mcqs.why: Divide both sides by 5: x = 3/5. The answer can be a fraction; it does not have to be a whole number.

mcqs.q: Solve: 4x + 10 = 2. What is x?
mcqs.why: Subtract 10 from both sides: 4x = 2 − 10 = −8. Then divide by 4: x = −2. Move the number first, then divide.

mcqs.q: Solve: 2 + 14x = 30. What is x?
mcqs.why: Subtract 2 from both sides: 14x = 28. Then divide by 14: x = 2. Check: 2 + 14 × 2 = 30, which is correct.

mcqs.q: Solve: 9 + 5x = 3x + 13. What is x?
mcqs.why: Subtract 3x from both sides: 9 + 2x = 13. Subtract 9: 2x = 4, so x = 2. Collect the x terms on one side first.

mcqs.q: Solve: 5 + 3(x − 1) = 5x − 6. What is x?
mcqs.why: Open the bracket: 5 + 3x − 3 = 5x − 6, so 3x + 2 = 5x − 6. Then 8 = 2x, so x = 4. Always open brackets before moving terms.

mcqs.q: Solve: 6x + 2 = 29 − 3x. What is x?
mcqs.why: Add 3x to both sides: 9x + 2 = 29. Subtract 2: 9x = 27, so x = 3. Bring all x terms to the left side.

mcqs.q: Solve: 3x/4 = 2/5. What is x?
mcqs.why: Multiply both sides by 20: 15x = 8, so x = 8/15. Multiplying by the LCM (20) removes both fractions at once.

mcqs.q: Solve: (x + 2)/3 = (1 − 2x)/5. What is x?
mcqs.why: Cross-multiply: 5(x + 2) = 3(1 − 2x), so 5x + 10 = 3 − 6x. Then 11x = −7, so x = −7/11. Cross-multiplication works when each side is a single fraction.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.2 — Solving and Checking Equations
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

Solving an equation is not finished until you check the answer. Put your value of x back into the left-hand side (LHS). If the LHS becomes equal to the right-hand side (RHS), your answer is correct.

This exercise also has fraction equations like (x + 3)/(x − 1) = 6/7, which are solved by cross-multiplying.

Formula / Rule

Solve first: move numbers, then divide to get x.

Check: put the value of x in the LHS and simplify. LHS must equal RHS.

For (a)/(b) = (c)/(d) type equations, cross-multiply first.

Worked Example

Solve and check: 3x + 9 = 18.

Step 1: Subtract 9 from both sides: 3x = 9.

Step 2: Divide both sides by 3: x = 3.

Step 3: Check: LHS = 3(3) + 9 = 18 = RHS. ✓ The answer is correct.

Remember

  • For 5x − 20 = 30, x = 10, and the check is 5(10) − 20 = 30. ✓
  • Answers can be fractions: 4x + 8 = 2 gives x = −3/2, and 4(−3/2) + 8 = 2. ✓
  • For (2x + 3)/(7x + 1) = 7/15, cross-multiplying gives x = 2, and (4 + 3)/(14 + 1) = 7/15. ✓

mcqs.q: Solve: 3x + 9 = 18. What is x?
mcqs.why: Subtract 9: 3x = 9, so x = 3. Check: LHS = 3(3) + 9 = 18 = RHS, so the answer is verified.

mcqs.q: Solve: 2x − 5 = 9. What is x?
mcqs.why: Add 5 to both sides: 2x = 14, so x = 7. Check: LHS = 2(7) − 5 = 9 = RHS, so x = 7 is correct.

mcqs.q: Solve: 5x − 20 = 30. What is x?
mcqs.why: Add 20 to both sides: 5x = 50, so x = 10. Check: LHS = 5(10) − 20 = 30 = RHS, which confirms the answer.

mcqs.q: Solve: 3x + 17 = 2. What is x?
mcqs.why: Subtract 17: 3x = −15, so x = −5. Check: LHS = 3(−5) + 17 = 2 = RHS. A negative answer is checked in the same way.

mcqs.q: Solve: 13 − 3x = −2. What is x?
mcqs.why: Subtract 13: −3x = −15, so x = 5. Check: LHS = 13 − 3(5) = −2 = RHS, so the answer is correct.

mcqs.q: Solve: 4x + 8 = 2. What is x?
Solve: (x + 3)/(x − 1) = 6/7. What is x?
Solve: 5x + 1 = 6/5. What is x?
Solve: (x − 1)/(x + 2) = 4/3. What is x?
Solve: (3x − 8)/(5x + 2) = 1. What is x?
mcqs.why: Multiply both sides by (5x + 2): 3x − 8 = 5x + 2, so −10 = 2x and x = −5. Check: (−15 − 8)/(−25 + 2) = (−23)/(−23) = 1 = RHS.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.3 — Word Problems with Equations
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

In word problems, first choose a letter for the unknown, usually x. Then change the words into an equation and solve it.

Common patterns: consecutive numbers are x, x + 1, x + 2; perimeter of a rectangle is 2(length + width); perimeter of a square is 4 × side; if one person has 4 times as much as another, write x and 4x.

Formula / Rule

Let the unknown be x. Write the equation from the words. Solve it. Then answer in words with units.

Perimeter of rectangle = 2 × (Length + Width)

Perimeter of square = 4 × Side

Worked Example

Two consecutive numbers have sum 43. Find the numbers.

Step 1: Let the first number be x, so the second is x + 1.

Step 2: Equation: x + (x + 1) = 43, so 2x + 1 = 43.

Step 3: 2x = 42, so x = 21.

Step 4: The numbers are 21 and 22.

Remember

  • Room problem: width x, length x + 1.5, perimeter 63 m gives width 15 m and length 16.5 m.
  • Hassan and Asghar: x + 4x = 800 gives Asghar Rs. 160 and Hassan Rs. 640.
  • The think-of-a-number trick (add 3, double, subtract 6, halve) always gives back the original number x.

mcqs.q: Ali had some rupees. Rs. 7 added to them makes Rs. 22. How many rupees did Ali have?
mcqs.why: Let Ali's amount be x. Equation: x + 7 = 22, so x = 15. Ali had Rs. 15, and 15 + 7 = 22 confirms it.

mcqs.q: Aslam bought 3 pencils and had Rs. 5 left from Rs. 35. How much does one pencil cost?
mcqs.why: Let one pencil cost x. Equation: 3x + 5 = 35, so 3x = 30 and x = 10. One pencil costs Rs. 10.

mcqs.q: A room's length is 1.5 m more than its width and its perimeter is 63 m. What are the length and width?
mcqs.why: Let width be x, length x + 1.5. Then 2(x + x + 1.5) = 63 gives 2x = 30, so x = 15. Width is 15 m and length is 15 + 1.5 = 16.5 m.

mcqs.q: A 32 cm wire is bent into a square. How long is each side?
mcqs.why: Let the side be x. Perimeter of a square: 4x = 32, so x = 8. Each side of the square is 8 cm.

mcqs.q: Hassan and Asghar together have Rs. 800. Hassan has 4 times as much as Asghar. How much does each have?
mcqs.why: Let Asghar have x, so Hassan has 4x. Then x + 4x = 800, so 5x = 800 and x = 160. Asghar has Rs. 160 and Hassan has 4 × 160 = Rs. 640.

mcqs.q: Think of a number, add 3, multiply by 2, subtract 6, then divide by 2. How does the final answer compare with the original number?
options: It is equal to the original number
It is 3 more than the original
mcqs.why: Let the number be x: x → x + 3 → 2x + 6 → 2x → x. Every step cancels out, so the final answer equals the original thought number.

mcqs.q: Two consecutive numbers have sum 43. What are they?
mcqs.why: Let the numbers be x and x + 1. Then 2x + 1 = 43, so x = 21. The two consecutive numbers are 21 and 22.

mcqs.q: Three consecutive numbers have sum 48. What are they?
mcqs.why: Let the numbers be x, x + 1, x + 2. Then 3x + 3 = 48, so x = 15. The three numbers are 15, 16 and 17.

mcqs.q: The 1/3 part and the 1/4 part of an amount add up to 14. What is the amount?
mcqs.why: Let the amount be x. Equation: x/3 + x/4 = 14. Multiply by 12: 4x + 3x = 168, so 7x = 168 and x = 24. The amount is 24.

mcqs.q: The sum of two numbers is 9. Five times the first minus four times the second is also 9. What are the numbers?
mcqs.why: Let the first be x, so the second is 9 − x. Then 5x − 4(9 − x) = 9 gives 9x = 45, so x = 5. The two numbers are 5 and 4.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 9 — Linear Equations: Mixed Practice
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

A linear equation in one variable has only one variable, and its power (degree) is 1. The value that makes both sides equal is called the solution, or root, of the equation.

Adding the same number to both sides does not change the equality. This is the key rule used in every solution.

This review also asks you to write equations for consecutive-number problems and to solve fraction equations by cross-multiplying.

Formula / Rule

Linear equation: one variable, degree 1. Example: 2x + 1 = 6 has degree 1.

Solution (root): the value of x that makes LHS = RHS. Example: x + 3 = 8 has solution x = 5.

Worked Example

Solve: (x + 1)/(x − 3) = 5/3.

Step 1: Cross-multiply: 3(x + 1) = 5(x − 3).

Step 2: Open brackets: 3x + 3 = 5x − 15.

Step 3: Subtract 3x from both sides: 3 = 2x − 15.

Step 4: Add 15 to both sides: 18 = 2x, so x = 9.

Remember

  • Three consecutive numbers with sum 21 are 6, 7 and 8; four with sum 46 are 10, 11, 12 and 13.
  • 1½x = 1 gives x = 2/3, because (3/2)x = 1 means x = 2/3.
  • A 120 cm wire bent into a rectangle with length 10 cm more than width gives width 25 cm and length 35 cm.

mcqs.q: An equation in which one variable is of power one is called a linear equation in _____.
mcqs.why: A linear equation in one variable has a single variable raised to power 1. The word linear comes from this power 1, the lowest degree of such an equation.

mcqs.q: The solution of an equation is also called its _____.
mcqs.why: The solution of an equation is also called its root. It is the value of the variable that makes both sides of the equation equal.

mcqs.q: What is the lowest degree (power) of a linear equation?
mcqs.why: The degree of a linear equation is 1, because the variable appears with power 1. For example, in 2x + 1 = 6 the power of x is 1.

mcqs.q: From the equation 1½x = 1, what is the value of x?
mcqs.why: Write 1½ as 3/2: (3/2)x = 1, so x = 1 ÷ (3/2) = 2/3. Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal.

mcqs.q: Solve: x/2 − 4 = 2. What is x?
mcqs.why: Add 4 to both sides: x/2 = 6. Multiply both sides by 2: x = 12. Check: 12/2 − 4 = 2, which is correct.

mcqs.q: Solve: (x − 7)/4 = 3. What is x?
mcqs.why: Multiply both sides by 4: x − 7 = 12. Add 7 to both sides: x = 19. Always clear the fraction first in this type of equation.

mcqs.q: Solve: (x − 2)/(x − 1) = 3/4. What is x?
mcqs.why: Cross-multiply: 4(x − 2) = 3(x − 1), so 4x − 8 = 3x − 3. Then x = 5. Check: (5 − 2)/(5 − 1) = 3/4, which matches.

mcqs.q: Solve: (x + 3)/3 = (x + 6)/2. What is x?
mcqs.why: Cross-multiply: 2(x + 3) = 3(x + 6), so 2x + 6 = 3x + 18. Then x = −12. The answer is negative here, which is perfectly possible.

mcqs.q: Three consecutive numbers have sum 21. What are they?
mcqs.why: Let the numbers be x, x + 1, x + 2. Then 3x + 3 = 21, so x = 6. The three numbers are 6, 7 and 8.

mcqs.q: A 120 cm wire is bent into a rectangle whose length is 10 cm more than its width. What are the length and width?
mcqs.why: Let width be x, length x + 10. Then 2(x + x + 10) = 120 gives 2x = 50, so x = 25. Width is 25 cm and length is 35 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.1 — Adjacent, Complementary and Supplementary Angles
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

Angles that share a vertex and a side are special. We learn to name them and to find missing angles.

Adjacent angles: Two angles with a common vertex and a common side, with the other sides on opposite sides of the common side.

Complementary angles: Two angles whose sum is 90°.

Supplementary angles: Two angles whose sum is 180°.

Vertically opposite angles: When two straight lines cross, the angles opposite each other are equal.

Formula / Rule

Complementary angle = 90° − given angle

Supplementary angle = 180° − given angle

Sum of angles of a triangle = 180°

Angles on a straight line sum to 180°

Worked Example

Find the remaining angle if m∠MON = 130° and m∠MOP = 50°.

Step 1: ∠MON = ∠MOP + ∠PON

Step 2: 130° = 50° + m∠PON

Step 3: m∠PON = 130° − 50° = 80°

Also: complementary angle of 49° = 90° − 49° = 41°, and supplementary angle of 80° = 180° − 80° = 100°.

Remember

  • If an angle equals its complement, the angle is 45°.
  • If an angle equals its supplement, the angle is 90°.
  • The supplement of an acute angle is always obtuse.
  • In complementary angles, each angle is acute.
  • If two lines cross and one angle is a right angle, all four angles are right angles.
  • Vertically opposite angles are equal, e.g. opposite 55° is also 55°, the other two are 125° each.

mcqs.q: What is the complementary angle of 49°?
mcqs.why: Complementary angles sum to 90°. So 90° − 49° = 41°. This is the rule used in Exercise 10.1 Q4 for all such questions.

mcqs.q: What is the supplementary angle of 80°?
mcqs.why: Supplementary angles sum to 180°. So 180° − 80° = 100°. Remember: complement uses 90°, supplement uses 180°.

mcqs.q: If m∠MON = 130° and m∠MOP = 50°, what is m∠PON?
mcqs.why: ∠MON = ∠MOP + ∠PON, so 130° = 50° + m∠PON. Therefore m∠PON = 130° − 50° = 80°. Adjacent angles add up to the whole angle.

mcqs.q: Two straight lines cross and one angle is 55°. What is its vertically opposite angle?
mcqs.why: Vertically opposite angles are equal. So the angle opposite 55° is also 55°. The neighbouring angles are 180° − 55° = 125° each.

mcqs.q: If an angle is equal to its complement, what is the angle?
mcqs.why: Let the angle be x. Then x = 90° − x, so 2x = 90° and x = 45°. An angle equal to its complement is always 45°.

mcqs.q: If an angle is equal to its supplement, what is the angle?
mcqs.why: Let the angle be x. Then x = 180° − x, so 2x = 180° and x = 90°. Only a right angle equals its own supplement.

mcqs.q: The supplement of an acute angle is always:
mcqs.why: An acute angle is less than 90°. Its supplement is 180° minus less than 90°, which is more than 90° and less than 180°, so it is obtuse.

mcqs.q: What is the complementary angle of 62°?
mcqs.why: Complementary angles sum to 90°. So 90° − 62° = 28°. This matches Exercise 10.1 Q4(ii) in the book.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, m∠B = 90° and exterior angle at C is 125°. What is m∠BAC?
mcqs.why: First m∠ACB = 180° − 125° = 55° on a straight line. Then angles of a triangle sum to 180°, so m∠BAC = 180° − 90° − 55° = 35°.

mcqs.q: What is the supplementary angle of 132°?
mcqs.why: Supplementary angles sum to 180°. So 180° − 132° = 48°. This is Exercise 10.1 Q5(ii) from the book.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.2 — Congruent and Similar Figures
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

Two figures can look alike in two ways.

Congruent figures: Same shape AND same measure (size). One figure exactly covers the other.

Similar figures: Same shape but different measure (size). One is a bigger or smaller copy of the other.

Every congruent pair is also similar, but similar figures are not always congruent.

Formula / Rule

Congruent: shape same + measure same

Similar: shape same + measure different

In similar figures, the ratio of corresponding sides is the same.

Worked Example

Two squares have the same shape but different measures. Are they congruent or similar?

Step 1: Check the shape — both are squares, so shape is same.

Step 2: Check the measure — measures are different.

Step 3: Same shape, different measure means the figures are similar, not congruent.

Two triangles with same shape and same measure are congruent.

Remember

  • Two circles are always similar; they are congruent only if radii are equal.
  • Line segments 3 cm and 5 cm are similar but not congruent.
  • Figures P and Q on the grid covering 6 cells with same shape are congruent; P is Q rotated 180°.
  • Figures P (5 × 2) and R (6 × 3) are neither congruent nor similar because the side ratio 5:2 is not equal to 6:3.
  • Currency notes of different values have same shape, so they are similar, but not congruent unless measures match.

mcqs.q: Two triangles have the same shape and the same measure. They are:
mcqs.why: Same shape plus same measure means congruent. Congruent figures exactly cover each other. They are also similar, but congruent is the stronger and correct name here.

mcqs.q: Two squares have the same shape but different measures. They are:
mcqs.why: Same shape with different measure means similar figures. They are not congruent because their sizes differ. All squares are similar to each other.

mcqs.q: Two circles with different radii are:
mcqs.why: All circles have the same shape, so circles are always similar. With different radii the measures differ, so they are not congruent.

mcqs.q: Two line segments, 3 cm and 5 cm long, are:
mcqs.why: Both are straight line segments, so the shape is the same, but lengths 3 cm and 5 cm are different. Hence they are similar, not congruent.

mcqs.q: Two parallelograms with same shape and same measure are:
mcqs.why: When both shape and measure are the same, figures are congruent. This is the definition used throughout Exercise 10.2.

mcqs.q: Figures P (5 cells by 2 cells) and R (6 cells by 3 cells) are:
mcqs.why: Ratio for P is 5:2 and for R is 6:3 = 2:1. The ratios are not equal, so they are not similar, and measures differ so they are not congruent either.

mcqs.q: Which statement is true?
mcqs.why: Congruent figures have same shape and same size, so they also satisfy the condition for similar figures. But similar figures may have different sizes, so they need not be congruent.

mcqs.q: Two rectangles with the same measures are:
mcqs.why: Same shape (rectangles) and same measures means the rectangles exactly match. So they are congruent, as in Exercise 10.2 Part B.

mcqs.q: The 10-rupee note and the 100-rupee note have the same shape. They are:
mcqs.why: The book states this is True: same shape means similar figures. Notes of different values differ in measure, so they are similar, not congruent.

mcqs.q: Two pentagons with same shape and same measure are:
mcqs.why: Same shape and same measure is the definition of congruent figures. Two such pentagons are congruent, as given in Exercise 10.2 Q1(ix).

lessons.title: Exercise 10.3 — Congruent Segments, Angles and Similar Figures
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

This exercise uses symbols. The symbol ≅ means congruent (same measure). The symbol ~ means similar.

Line segments of equal length are congruent. Angles of equal measure are congruent.

Two circles are congruent when their radii (or diameters) are equal.

Figures of different types, like an oval and a circle, or a circle and a semicircle, are neither similar nor congruent.

Formula / Rule

AB ≅ XY means mAB = mXY

In similar figures: ratio of corresponding sides is equal

Worked Example

Similar triangles PQE and XYZ: PQ = 4 cm, XY = 8 cm, PE = 6 cm, YZ = 14 cm. Find QE (x) and XZ (y).

Step 1: Ratio = XY ÷ PQ = 8 ÷ 4 = 2

Step 2: x = QE = YZ ÷ 2 = 14 ÷ 2 = 7 cm

Step 3: y = XZ = 2 × PE = 2 × 6 = 12 cm

Another example: trapeziums with ratio 10/5 = 2 give y = 2 × 4 = 8 cm and x = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm.

Remember

  • Equal segments: AB ≅ XY (3.2 cm), DE ≅ XZ (5.1 cm), MN ≅ CD (4.5 cm), RS ≅ PQ (5.4 cm).
  • Equal angles: ∠ABC ≅ ∠PRQ (60°), ∠XYZ ≅ ∠MNS (110°), ∠COD ≅ ∠PQR (45°), ∠AOB ≅ ∠DEF (70°).
  • If ∠ABC ≅ ∠DEF and m∠ABC = 100°, then m∠DEF = 100°.
  • Acute-angled and right-angled triangles are different types, so neither similar nor congruent.

mcqs.q: If mAB = 3.2 cm and mXY = 3.2 cm, then:
mcqs.why: Line segments of equal measure are congruent, written AB ≅ XY. The symbol ≅ is used for congruent segments and angles of equal measure.

mcqs.q: If m∠ABC = 60° and m∠PRQ = 60°, then:
mcqs.why: Angles of equal measure are congruent. Both are 60°, so ∠ABC ≅ ∠PRQ. This pair is given in Exercise 10.3 Q3.

mcqs.q: Two circles are congruent when their ___ are equal.
mcqs.why: A circle is fixed by its radius or diameter. If diameters (or radii) are equal, the circles have same shape and same measure, so they are congruent.

mcqs.q: An oval and a circle are:
mcqs.why: Their types are different — an oval is not a circle. Figures of different types are neither similar nor congruent.

mcqs.q: Similar triangles ABC and DEF: BC/EF = 5/3, AC = x, DF = 5 cm. What is x?
mcqs.why: In similar triangles ratios are equal: 5/3 = x/5, so x = 25/3 = 8.33 cm approximately. This is Exercise 10.3 Q5(i) from the book.

mcqs.q: In similar triangles PQE and XYZ, ratio XY/PQ = 2 and PE = 6 cm. What is XZ?
mcqs.why: Corresponding sides are in ratio 2, so XZ = 2 × PE = 2 × 6 = 12 cm. Always multiply by the same ratio for corresponding sides.

mcqs.q: If m∠ABC = 100° and ∠ABC ≅ ∠DEF, then m∠DEF is:
mcqs.why: Congruent angles have equal measures. Since ∠ABC ≅ ∠DEF, m∠DEF = m∠ABC = 100°. This is Exercise 10.3 Q4(i).

mcqs.q: Two rhombuses with same type but different measures are:
mcqs.why: Same type (shape) but different measure means similar figures. They are not congruent because sizes differ.

mcqs.q: A circle and a semicircle are:
mcqs.why: A circle and a semicircle are figures of different types. So they are neither similar nor congruent, as stated in Exercise 10.3 Q1(ix).

mcqs.q: Larger trapezium is twice the smaller. Smaller top side is 4 cm. Larger top side y is:
mcqs.why: Ratio is 10/5 = 2, so larger = 2 × smaller. y = 2 × 4 = 8 cm. The bottom side x = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm in the same question.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.4 — Congruence of Triangles: SSS, SAS, ASA, HS
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

Two triangles are congruent if enough equal parts are known. There are four rules.

SSS: Three sides equal.

SAS: Two sides and the included angle equal.

ASA: Two angles and the included side equal.

HS: In right triangles, hypotenuse and one side equal.

A diagonal of a rectangle or parallelogram divides it into two congruent triangles.

Formula / Rule

SSS: side-side-side

SAS: side-angle-side (angle between the sides)

ASA: angle-side-angle (side between the angles)

HS: hypotenuse-side (right triangles only)

Worked Example

Triangles APC and BPD: AP ≅ BP, CP ≅ DP, angles at P are vertically opposite. Which rule?

Step 1: Two pairs of sides are equal: AP ≅ BP and CP ≅ DP.

Step 2: The included angles ∠APC and ∠BPD are equal (vertically opposite).

Step 3: Two sides + included angle = SAS property. So ΔAPC ≅ ΔBPD by SAS.

Remember

  • Rectangle PQRS with diagonal PR: ΔPQR ≅ ΔRSP by SSS.
  • Parallelogram ABCD with diagonal BD: ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB by ASA.
  • Right triangles with equal hypotenuse and one side use HS, e.g. ΔPQO ≅ ΔMNO.
  • Common side counts as equal in both triangles.

mcqs.q: ΔAPC ≅ ΔBPD with AP ≅ BP, CP ≅ DP and vertically opposite angles at P. The property is:
mcqs.why: Two sides are equal and the angle between them (vertically opposite at P) is equal. That is the SAS — side-angle-side — property.

mcqs.q: Both are right triangles, hypotenuses PO ≅ MO and QO ≅ NO. The property is:
mcqs.why: HS is for right triangles: Hypotenuse and one Side equal. Both conditions are given, so ΔPQO ≅ ΔMNO by HS.

mcqs.q: In rectangle PQRS, diagonal PR gives ΔPQR ≅ ΔRSP by:
mcqs.why: PQ ≅ RS, QR ≅ SP (opposite sides of rectangle) and PR is common. Three sides equal means SSS property.

mcqs.q: ∠A ≅ ∠D, ∠B ≅ ∠E and AC ≅ DC. ΔABC ≅ ΔDEC by:
mcqs.why: Two angles and the included side AC/DC are equal. That is the ASA — angle-side-angle — property.

mcqs.q: PQ ≅ PO, QR ≅ OR and PR is common. ΔPQR ≅ ΔPOR by:
mcqs.why: All three sides match: two given pairs plus the common side PR. Three equal sides means SSS property.

mcqs.q: In parallelogram ABCD, diagonal BD, ∠ABD ≅ ∠CDB, ∠ADB ≅ ∠CBD, BD common. Property is:
mcqs.why: Two angles and the included common side BD are equal. That is ASA. A diagonal divides a parallelogram into two congruent triangles.

mcqs.q: AC ≅ CD, BC ≅ CE and angles at C are vertically opposite. Property is:
mcqs.why: Two sides AC, BC match CD, CE and the included angles at C are vertically opposite and equal. So SAS applies to ΔACB ≅ ΔDCE.

mcqs.q: RQ ≅ SQ, right angles at Q, PQ common. ΔPQR ≅ ΔPQS by:
mcqs.why: The book gives this as SAS: side RQ ≅ SQ, the right angle at Q is the included angle, and PQ is the common side.

mcqs.q: CD ≅ FE, right angles at D and E, DE common. ΔCDE ≅ ΔFED by:
mcqs.why: Side CD ≅ FE, right angles at D and E are equal, and DE is a common side. The book classifies this as SAS property.

mcqs.q: HS property is used only for:
mcqs.why: HS stands for Hypotenuse-Side and hypotenuse exists only in a right triangle. So HS applies only when both triangles are right-angled.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.5 — Parts of a Circle: Radius, Diameter, Chord
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

A circle is the set of points at an equal distance from a fixed point called the centre.

Radius: Distance from centre to any point on the circle; also the segment joining centre to a point on the circle.

Chord: Segment joining two points on the circle.

Diameter: The chord which passes through the centre. It is the longest chord.

Segment: A chord divides the circle into a major segment and a minor segment.

Formula / Rule

Diameter = 2 × radius

Radius = diameter ÷ 2 = half of diameter

Worked Example

If radius is 7 cm, what is the diameter?

Step 1: Diameter passes through the centre and is twice the radius.

Step 2: Diameter = 2 × 7 = 14 cm

Step 3: Radius = half of diameter = 14 ÷ 2 = 7 cm (check)

All radii of a circle are equal in measure and length; all diameters are also equal.

Remember

  • All points of a circle are at equal distance from the centre.
  • A circle has many radii and many diameters, all equal within the same circle.
  • The diameter passes through the centre.
  • The chord through the centre is the diameter.

mcqs.q: A line segment joining two points on a circle is called a:
mcqs.why: By definition in Exercise 10.5 Q1, a segment joining two points on the circle is a chord. If it passes through the centre it becomes the diameter.

mcqs.q: The distance from the centre to any point on the circle is called the:
mcqs.why: That distance is the radius. Every point on the circle is at this same distance — the radius — from the centre.

mcqs.q: The chord which passes through the centre is called the:
mcqs.why: A chord through the centre is the diameter. The diameter is the longest chord of the circle.

mcqs.q: The diameter is ___ the radius.
mcqs.why: Diameter = 2 × radius. It passes through the centre, joining two points on the circle, so it contains two radii.

mcqs.q: The radius is ___ of the diameter.
mcqs.why: Radius = diameter ÷ 2, i.e. half of the diameter. This is Exercise 10.5 Q9 in the book.

mcqs.q: All points of a circle are at equal distance from the:
mcqs.why: That equal distance is the radius, measured from the centre. This is the defining property of a circle.

mcqs.q: The major and minor parts made by a chord are called:
mcqs.why: A chord divides the circle into two segments — the major segment (bigger part) and the minor segment (smaller part).

mcqs.q: The diameters of a circle are many but equal in:
mcqs.why: Exercise 10.5 Q10: diameters are many but equal to each other in measure and length, just like radii in Q8.

mcqs.q: The segment joining the centre to a point on the circle is the:
mcqs.why: Centre to circle point is the radius (Q3). A segment joining two points on the circle would be a chord instead.

mcqs.q: The diameter passes through the:
mcqs.why: By definition the diameter passes through the centre of the circle. That is what makes it a special chord.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.6 — Angles in a Semicircle and in the Same Segment
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

This is practical work with compass and protractor. Two facts are found by measuring.

Angle in a semicircle: Join any point on the arc of a semicircle to both ends of the diameter. The angle formed is always 90° — a right angle.

Angles in the same segment: Join two different points in the same segment to both ends of a chord. The angles formed are equal.

Formula / Rule

Angle in a semicircle = 90°

Angles in the same segment are equal

Worked Example

Draw a semicircle of radius 2.5 cm and measure the angle in it.

Step 1: Draw the semicircle with compass, radius 2.5 cm.

Step 2: Take any point on the arc and join it to both ends of the diameter.

Step 3: Measure with a protractor — the angle is 90°.

Step 4: Repeat with radius 3 cm and radius 3.3 cm — every time the angle is 90°.

Remember

  • The result does not depend on radius: 2.5 cm, 3 cm, 3.3 cm all give 90°.
  • For same segment, circles of radius 2.7 cm, 2.8 cm and 3.4 cm were used — angles in the same segment were equal each time.
  • Angles in the major segment are equal to each other, and angles in the minor segment are equal to each other.

mcqs.q: The angle in a semicircle is always:
mcqs.why: By measuring semicircles of radii 2.5 cm and 3 cm, the angle formed at any point on the arc is 90°. The angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

mcqs.q: In a semicircle of radius 3.3 cm, every angle in the semicircle is:
mcqs.why: Exercise 10.6 Q2 checks two or three different points on the arc. Every angle measures 90°, so every angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

mcqs.q: Angles in the same segment of a circle are:
mcqs.why: With a circle of radius 2.7 cm, angles formed in the same segment by joining points to the chord ends have equal measures. This is the second key fact of Exercise 10.6.

mcqs.q: To check the angle in a semicircle, we join a point on the arc to:
options: Both ends of any chord only
mcqs.why: The method in Q1 and Q2: join any point on the arc to both ends of the diameter, then measure. The angle at the arc point is the angle in the semicircle.

mcqs.q: In a circle of radius 2.8 cm, the two angles in the major segment are:
mcqs.why: Q4 draws two angles in each segment. The two angles of the major segment are equal to each other, and the two of the minor segment are also equal to each other.

mcqs.q: What instrument is used to measure the angles in Exercise 10.6?
mcqs.why: Circles are drawn with a compass, but angles are measured with a protractor. The observation of 90° and equal angles comes from protractor measurement.

mcqs.q: A semicircle for Q1 was drawn with radii:
mcqs.why: Q1 specifically uses radii 2.5 cm and 3 cm. Both semicircles give the same result: angle = 90°, showing radius does not change the result.

mcqs.q: For same-segment angles, Q3 uses a circle of radius:
mcqs.why: Exercise 10.6 Q3 draws a circle of radius 2.7 cm, draws a chord, and shows angles in the same segment are equal.

mcqs.q: Q5 uses a circle of radius 3.4 cm to check that two angles in the same segment are:
mcqs.why: Q5 repeats the same-segment test with radius 3.4 cm. The two angles measured are equal, confirming the rule again.

mcqs.q: If a triangle is drawn with diameter as base and third point on the semicircle, the angle opposite the diameter is:
mcqs.why: That angle is the angle in a semicircle. By all measurements in Exercise 10.6 it is 90°, a right angle, whatever the radius.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 10 — Geometry: Mixed Review
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

This review joins all of Unit 10: angle pairs, congruent and similar figures, triangle congruence, and circle facts.

Adjacent angles: Common vertex and common side.

Complementary: Sum 90° (e.g. 30° and 60°). Supplementary: Sum 180° (e.g. 50° and 130°).

Vertically opposite angles: Formed when two lines cross; they are equal.

Similar (~): Same shape, different measure. Congruent (≅): Same shape and same measure.

Formula / Rule

Complementary sum = 90°

Supplementary sum = 180°

Diameter = 2 × radius

Angle in a semicircle = 90°

Worked Example

Parallelogram ABCD, diagonal AC. Prove ΔABC ≅ ΔCDA.

Step 1: Opposite sides equal: AB ≅ CD and BC ≅ DA.

Step 2: AC is a common side.

Step 3: Three sides equal, so ΔABC ≅ ΔCDA by SSS.

Also: a semicircle of radius 4.4 cm with triangle ABC on diameter AB gives ∠ACB = 90°.

Remember

  • Circle parts: centre, radius, diameter, chord, arc, major arc, minor arc, semicircle, segment.
  • Angles in the same segment are equal — checked for minor segment (radius 3.6 cm) and major segment (radius 4 cm).
  • HS property: hypotenuse and one side equal in right triangles gives congruence.

mcqs.q: Angles with a common vertex and a common side are called:
mcqs.why: Review Q12(i): angles which have one vertex and one common side are adjacent angles. Their other sides lie on opposite sides of the common side.

mcqs.q: If the sum of two angles is 90°, they are called:
mcqs.why: Complementary angles sum to 90°, e.g. 30° and 60° in Review Q2. Supplementary angles sum to 180° instead.

mcqs.q: 50° and 130° are an example of:
mcqs.why: 50° + 130° = 180°, so they are supplementary angles. This exact example is given in Review Exercise 10 Q2.

mcqs.q: Similar figures have:
mcqs.why: Review Q12(iii) and Q4: similar figures have the same shape but different measure. The symbol for similar is ~.

mcqs.q: The symbol for congruent figures is:
mcqs.why: Congruent is written with ≅, e.g. ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF. The symbol ~ is for similar figures. Do not mix the two symbols.

mcqs.q: Parallelogram ABCD with diagonal AC: ΔABC ≅ ΔCDA by which property?
mcqs.why: AB ≅ CD, BC ≅ DA (opposite sides) and AC is common. Three equal sides means SSS property, as proved in Review Q7.

mcqs.q: In a semicircle of radius 4.4 cm, triangle ABC on diameter AB has ∠ACB equal to:
mcqs.why: ∠ACB is the angle in a semicircle, so it is 90°. Note the book printed ∠ABC, which is a printing error; the angle at C is the right angle.

mcqs.q: Vertically opposite angles are:
mcqs.why: Review Q12(iv): when two lines cut each other, the vertically opposite angles formed are equal and congruent to each other.

mcqs.q: Angles in the minor segment of a circle (radius 3.6 cm) are:
mcqs.why: Review Q10 checks this with radius 3.6 cm. Two angles in the minor segment have equal measures, just like in the major segment.

mcqs.q: In a right triangle, hypotenuse and one side congruent to the other right triangle gives congruence by:
mcqs.why: Review Q12(v) describes the HS property: Hypotenuse and Side equal in two right triangles makes them congruent.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.1 — Dividing a Line Segment
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

In this exercise we divide a line segment into equal parts, or into parts in a given ratio, using only a ruler and a compass. We do not measure the small parts with a ruler; the construction itself makes them equal.

Instruments used: ruler (to draw lines) and compass (to mark equal arcs). Parallels are drawn with set squares or by copying angles.

Formula / Rule

Each equal part = Length of segment ÷ Number of parts

For ratio a : b, first part = a ÷ (a + b) × Length, second part = b ÷ (a + b) × Length

Construction Steps — Worked Example

Divide a 6 cm line segment into 4 equal parts.

Step 1: Draw a line segment 6 cm long with a ruler.

Step 2: From one end, draw a ray at an acute angle (about 40°).

Step 3: With a compass, mark 4 equal arcs on the ray.

Step 4: Join the fourth mark to the other end of the segment.

Step 5: Draw parallels to this joining line through the other marks, cutting the segment.

Step 6: Each part = 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 cm. All four parts are 1.5 cm each.

Remember

  • For ratio 2 : 3 on 5 cm, mark 2 + 3 = 5 arcs; the parts are 2 cm and 3 cm.
  • For ratio 1 : 2 : 3 on 6.6 cm, mark 6 arcs; the parts are 1.1 cm, 2.2 cm and 3.3 cm.
  • The number of arcs always equals the total of the ratio parts (or the number of equal parts).

mcqs.q: A 6 cm line segment is divided into 4 equal parts. How long is each part?
mcqs.why: Each part = 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 cm. The construction uses a ray at an acute angle, 4 equal compass arcs, and parallel lines to cut the segment equally.

mcqs.q: Line segment AB = 7.5 cm is divided into 5 equal parts. How long is each part?
mcqs.why: Each part = 7.5 ÷ 5 = 1.5 cm. Mark 5 equal arcs on the ray, join the fifth mark to B, and draw parallels through the other marks.

mcqs.q: Line segment CD = 9 cm is divided into 4 equal parts. How long is each part?
mcqs.why: Each part = 9 ÷ 4 = 2.25 cm. Dividing a length by the number of parts always gives the size of one part.

mcqs.q: A 5 cm segment is divided in the ratio 2 : 3. What are the two parts?
mcqs.why: Total parts = 2 + 3 = 5. First part = (2/5) × 5 = 2 cm and second part = (3/5) × 5 = 3 cm. Mark 5 arcs and draw a parallel through the 2nd mark.

mcqs.q: An 8.4 cm segment is divided in the ratio 1 : 5. What are the two parts?
mcqs.why: Total parts = 1 + 5 = 6. First part = (1/6) × 8.4 = 1.4 cm and second part = (5/6) × 8.4 = 7 cm. Six equal arcs are marked on the ray.

mcqs.q: Segment MN = 7 cm is divided in the ratio 3 : 5. What is the first part?
mcqs.why: Total parts = 3 + 5 = 8. First part = (3/8) × 7 = 2.625 cm and second part = (5/8) × 7 = 4.375 cm. A parallel is drawn through the 3rd of the 8 marks.

mcqs.q: A 6.6 cm segment is divided in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. What are the three parts?
mcqs.why: Total parts = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. Parts are (1/6) × 6.6 = 1.1 cm, (2/6) × 6.6 = 2.2 cm and (3/6) × 6.6 = 3.3 cm. Parallels go through the 1st and 3rd marks.

mcqs.q: Segment XY = 7 cm is divided in the ratio 2 : 2 : 3. What are the three parts?
mcqs.why: Total parts = 2 + 2 + 3 = 7. Parts are (2/7) × 7 = 2 cm, (2/7) × 7 = 2 cm and (3/7) × 7 = 3 cm. Parallels go through the 2nd and 4th marks.

mcqs.q: An 8.4 cm segment is divided in the ratio 4 : 2 : 1. What is the largest part?
mcqs.why: Total parts = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7. The parts are (4/7) × 8.4 = 4.8 cm, (2/7) × 8.4 = 2.4 cm and (1/7) × 8.4 = 1.2 cm. The largest ratio number gives the largest part.

mcqs.q: In this construction, at what kind of angle is the ray drawn from one end of the segment?
mcqs.why: The book's method draws a ray at an acute angle, about 40°, from one end of the segment. Equal arcs are then marked on this ray with a compass.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.2 — Triangles from Perimeter and Ratio
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

Here the perimeter of a triangle and the ratio of its sides are given. First find the three sides by dividing a segment equal to the perimeter in the given ratio (the Exercise 11.1 method). Then construct the triangle with ruler and compass.

Important: a triangle is possible only if the sum of any two sides is greater than the third side. This is called the triangle inequality.

Formula / Rule

Each side = Its ratio part ÷ Total of ratio parts × Perimeter

Triangle rule: sum of two smaller sides must be greater than the largest side.

Construction Steps — Worked Example

Construct triangle DEF with perimeter 8.4 cm and sides in ratio 2 : 3 : 3.

Step 1: Draw a segment 8.4 cm long and divide it in the ratio 2 : 3 : 3.

Step 2: The sides are (2/8) × 8.4 = 2.1 cm, (3/8) × 8.4 = 3.15 cm and 3.15 cm.

Step 3: Draw the base 2.1 cm with a ruler.

Step 4: With a compass, draw an arc of 3.15 cm from one end and an arc of 3.15 cm from the other end.

Step 5: Join the point where the arcs meet to both ends. Triangle DEF is formed.

Remember

  • Ratio 1 : 2 : 3 with perimeter 9.6 cm gives sides 1.6, 3.2 and 4.8 cm — but 1.6 + 3.2 = 4.8, so NO triangle can be formed.
  • Ratio 5 : 3 : 2 with perimeter 10 cm gives 5, 3 and 2 cm — but 3 + 2 = 5, so NO triangle can be formed.
  • Ratio 2 : 3 : 4 with perimeter 90 mm gives sides 20 mm, 30 mm and 40 mm, and the triangle can be formed.

mcqs.q: Triangle DEF has perimeter 8.4 cm and sides in ratio 2 : 3 : 3. What are its sides?
mcqs.why: Total parts = 8. Sides are (2/8) × 8.4 = 2.1 cm and (3/8) × 8.4 = 3.15 cm twice. Then arcs of 3.15 cm from both ends of the 2.1 cm base complete the triangle.

mcqs.q: Triangle LMN has perimeter 90 mm and sides in ratio 2 : 3 : 4. What are its sides?
mcqs.why: Total parts = 9. Sides are (2/9) × 90 = 20 mm, (3/9) × 90 = 30 mm and (4/9) × 90 = 40 mm. Draw the 20 mm base, then arcs of 30 mm and 40 mm.

mcqs.q: Triangle XYZ has perimeter 88 mm and sides in ratio 3 : 3 : 2. What are its sides?
mcqs.why: Total parts = 8. Sides are (3/8) × 88 = 33 mm, 33 mm and (2/8) × 88 = 22 mm. The base is 22 mm with arcs of 33 mm from both ends.

mcqs.q: Sides in ratio 1 : 2 : 3 with perimeter 9.6 cm are 1.6 cm, 3.2 cm and 4.8 cm. Can a triangle be formed?
options: No, because 1.6 + 3.2 = 4.8, so the triangle inequality fails
mcqs.why: The sum of the two smaller sides must be greater than the largest side. Here 1.6 + 3.2 = 4.8, which only equals the largest side, so no triangle can be formed.

mcqs.q: Sides in ratio 5 : 3 : 2 with perimeter 10 cm are 5 cm, 3 cm and 2 cm. Can a triangle be formed?
options: Only if the base is 2 cm
No, because 3 + 2 = 5, so the triangle inequality fails
mcqs.why: Here 3 + 2 = 5, equal to the largest side, not greater than it. The triangle inequality is not satisfied, so the triangle is impossible with these numbers.

mcqs.q: What is the first step in constructing a triangle from its perimeter and the ratio of its sides?
options: Measure the angles with a protractor
Draw a segment equal to the perimeter and divide it in the given ratio
mcqs.why: First draw a line segment equal to the perimeter and divide it in the given ratio, as in Exercise 11.1. This gives the three side lengths needed for the construction.

mcqs.q: In triangle DEF (perimeter 8.4 cm, ratio 2 : 3 : 3), which length is used as the base?
mcqs.why: The base drawn first is 2.1 cm, the smallest side. Arcs of 3.15 cm are then drawn from both ends of this base with a compass.

mcqs.q: Which instrument is used to draw the arcs that locate the third vertex of the triangle?
mcqs.why: A compass draws the arcs of the two side lengths from the ends of the base. Where the arcs cross is the third vertex, which is joined to both ends.

mcqs.q: For triangle LMN (20 mm, 30 mm, 40 mm), why can the triangle be formed?
options: Because 20 + 30 = 50 is greater than 40, so the triangle inequality holds
mcqs.why: The triangle inequality needs the sum of the two smaller sides to be greater than the largest side. Here 20 + 30 = 50 > 40, so the construction works.

mcqs.q: A triangle's sides are in ratio 3 : 3 : 2 with perimeter 88 mm. What total is used to share out the perimeter?
mcqs.why: The total of the ratio parts is 3 + 3 + 2 = 8. Each side is its ratio number divided by 8, multiplied by the perimeter 88 mm.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.3 — Equilateral Triangles
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal and all three angles equal to 60°. It can be constructed in two ways: when the side is given, and when the altitude (height) is given.

The altitude of an equilateral triangle goes from a vertex straight down to the middle of the opposite side. It bisects (cuts into two equal parts) both the base and the 60° vertex angle, making 30° on each side.

Formula / Rule

Side given: draw the base, draw arcs of the same length from both ends, join the crossing point.

Altitude given: side = 2 × Altitude ÷ √3, using √3 ≈ 1.732

Construction Steps — Worked Example

Construct an equilateral triangle with side 2.9 cm.

Step 1: Draw a base 2.9 cm long with a ruler.

Step 2: Open the compass to 2.9 cm.

Step 3: Draw an arc from one end of the base and an arc from the other end.

Step 4: Join the point where the arcs meet to both ends of the base.

Step 5: All three sides are 2.9 cm. The equilateral triangle is formed.

Remember

  • For altitude 3.6 cm: draw a perpendicular at the midpoint of a base line, mark 3.6 cm on it, and make 30°–30° angles at the vertex. Side ≈ 4.16 cm.
  • Triangle PQR with side 50 mm uses the same arc method with the compass opened to 50 mm.
  • Triangle MNO with altitude 36 mm has side = 2 × 36 ÷ 1.732 ≈ 41.6 mm.

mcqs.q: To construct an equilateral triangle with side 3.2 cm, to what length do you open the compass for the arcs?
mcqs.why: Open the compass to 3.2 cm, the same as the side, and draw arcs from both ends of the 3.2 cm base. In an equilateral triangle all three sides are equal, so one compass opening does all the work.

mcqs.q: In an equilateral triangle, what is each angle?
mcqs.why: Each angle of an equilateral triangle is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°. All three sides are equal and all three angles are equal.

mcqs.q: An equilateral triangle has altitude 3.6 cm. About what is its side? (Side = 2 × Altitude ÷ 1.732)
mcqs.why: Side = 2 × 3.6 ÷ 1.732 = 7.2 ÷ 1.732 ≈ 4.16 cm. The altitude method uses 30°–30° angles at the vertex, because the altitude bisects the 60° angle.

mcqs.q: When constructing an equilateral triangle from its altitude, what angles are made at the vertex on both sides of the perpendicular?
mcqs.why: Angles of 30°–30° are made at the vertex on both sides of the perpendicular. This is because the altitude bisects the 60° vertex angle into two halves of 30° each.

mcqs.q: Triangle PQR has side 50 mm. How is it constructed?
options: Draw base QR 50 mm, draw arcs of 50 mm from Q and R, join the crossing point to Q and R
Draw any base and measure angles of 50°
mcqs.why: Draw base QR = 50 mm, open the compass to 50 mm and draw arcs from Q and R. Joining the intersection point to Q and R forms equilateral triangle PQR with all sides 50 mm.

mcqs.q: An equilateral triangle has altitude 4.5 cm. About what is its side?
mcqs.why: Side = 2 × 4.5 ÷ 1.732 = 9 ÷ 1.732 ≈ 5.20 cm. The side is always longer than the altitude in an equilateral triangle.

mcqs.q: Triangle MNO has altitude 36 mm. About what is its side?
mcqs.why: Side = 2 × 36 ÷ 1.732 = 72 ÷ 1.732 ≈ 41.57 mm, about 41.6 mm. Vertex M is marked 36 mm up the perpendicular, then 30°–30° rays find N and O.

mcqs.q: What does the altitude of an equilateral triangle bisect?
options: Both the base and the vertex angle
mcqs.why: The altitude bisects the base (it meets the base at its midpoint, at a right angle) and also bisects the vertex angle. That is why the 30°–30° construction works.

mcqs.q: To construct an equilateral triangle with side 4.3 cm, what is drawn first?
mcqs.why: First draw a base 4.3 cm long. Then open the compass to 4.3 cm, draw arcs from both ends, and join the crossing point to both ends.

mcqs.q: An equilateral triangle has altitude 4.8 cm. About what is its side?
mcqs.why: Side = 2 × 4.8 ÷ 1.732 = 9.6 ÷ 1.732 ≈ 5.54 cm. Use the formula side = 2 × altitude ÷ √3 with √3 ≈ 1.732 for every altitude question.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.4 — Isosceles Triangles
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

An isosceles triangle has two equal sides and two equal base angles. The angle between the two equal sides is called the vertex angle. The altitude from the vertex bisects the vertex angle and the base.

Three kinds of construction appear: base + base angle (use a protractor at both ends of the base), vertex angle + altitude, and altitude + base angle.

Formula / Rule

Vertex angle = 180° − 2 × Base angle

Base angle = (180° − Vertex angle) ÷ 2

At the vertex, the altitude makes angles of (Vertex angle ÷ 2) on each side.

Construction Steps — Worked Example

Construct an isosceles triangle with base 4.2 cm and base angle 42°.

Step 1: Draw a base 4.2 cm long with a ruler.

Step 2: At one end of the base, make a 42° angle with a protractor.

Step 3: At the other end of the base, make a 42° angle with a protractor.

Step 4: Join the point where the two rays meet to both ends of the base.

Step 5: The vertex angle is 180° − 2 × 42° = 96°.

Remember

  • Base 45 mm with base angle 45° gives vertex angle 180° − 90° = 90° — a right angle at the top.
  • Vertex angle 76° with altitude 4 cm: make 38°–38° at the vertex (76° ÷ 2); base angles are 52°.
  • Altitude 4.5 cm with base angle 54° gives vertex angle 180° − 2 × 54° = 72°.

mcqs.q: An isosceles triangle has base 4.2 cm and base angle 42°. What is its vertex angle?
mcqs.why: Vertex angle = 180° − 2 × 42° = 180° − 84° = 96°. The two base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal, so both are subtracted.

mcqs.q: An isosceles triangle has base angle 48°. What is its vertex angle?
mcqs.why: Vertex angle = 180° − 2 × 48° = 180° − 96° = 84°. This triangle has base 4.8 cm with 48° angles made at both ends using a protractor.

mcqs.q: An isosceles triangle has base 45 mm and base angle 45°. What is its vertex angle?
mcqs.why: Vertex angle = 180° − 2 × 45° = 180° − 90° = 90°. When both base angles are 45°, the vertex angle is a right angle.

mcqs.q: Which instrument is used to make the base angles in the base + base angle construction?
mcqs.why: A protractor makes the equal base angles at both ends of the base. The two rays meet at the vertex of the isosceles triangle.

mcqs.q: An isosceles triangle has vertex angle 76° and altitude 4 cm. What angles are made at the vertex on both sides of the perpendicular?
mcqs.why: The altitude bisects the vertex angle, so 76° ÷ 2 = 38° is made on each side of the perpendicular. The base angles are then (180° − 76°) ÷ 2 = 52°.

mcqs.q: An isosceles triangle has vertex angle 80°. What is each base angle?
mcqs.why: Base angle = (180° − 80°) ÷ 2 = 100° ÷ 2 = 50°. The two base angles share what is left of 180° equally.

mcqs.q: An isosceles triangle has vertex angle 100° and altitude 60 mm. What is each base angle?
mcqs.why: Base angle = (180° − 100°) ÷ 2 = 80° ÷ 2 = 40°. At the vertex, 100° ÷ 2 = 50°–50° angles are made on both sides of the perpendicular.

mcqs.q: An isosceles triangle has altitude 4.5 cm and base angle 54°. What is its vertex angle?
mcqs.why: Vertex angle = 180° − 2 × 54° = 180° − 108° = 72°. The vertex is marked 4.5 cm up the perpendicular and rays are drawn to make 54° at the base.

mcqs.q: An isosceles triangle has base angle 70° (altitude 4.7 cm). What is its vertex angle?
mcqs.why: Vertex angle = 180° − 2 × 70° = 180° − 140° = 40°. A large base angle leaves only a small angle at the vertex.

mcqs.q: An isosceles triangle has base angle 75° (altitude 59 mm). What is its vertex angle?
mcqs.why: Vertex angle = 180° − 2 × 75° = 180° − 150° = 30°. This is the smallest vertex angle in this exercise because the base angle is the largest.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.5 — Constructing Parallelograms
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

A parallelogram has opposite sides parallel and equal. This exercise constructs one in two ways.

Part A: two sides and the included angle are given. Draw one side, make the angle with a protractor, mark the second side, then use compass arcs to find the fourth corner.

Part B: two sides and a diagonal are given. Draw the diagonal first, build a triangle on it with compass arcs, then repeat the arcs on the other side of the diagonal to find the fourth corner.

Formula / Rule

Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal: the fourth corner is found with arcs equal to the two given sides.

Triangle check: the two sides and the diagonal must satisfy: sum of two sides > diagonal.

Construction Steps — Worked Example

Construct parallelogram PQRS with PQ = 5.9 cm, QR = 4.1 cm and angle PQR = 65°.

Step 1: Draw side PQ 5.9 cm long.

Step 2: At Q, make a 65° angle with a protractor.

Step 3: On that ray, mark side QR 4.1 cm long.

Step 4: Draw an arc from P equal to QR (4.1 cm) and an arc from R equal to PQ (5.9 cm) with a compass.

Step 5: Join the point where the arcs meet to P and R. Parallelogram PQRS is formed.

Remember

  • Part B example: BC = 6 cm, CD = 4 cm, diagonal BD = 7.3 cm — draw BD first; 6 + 4 > 7.3, so the triangle is possible.
  • Units must match: diagonal TR = 7.5 cm = 75 mm is used with sides 59 mm and 36 mm.
  • In Part B the same two arcs are drawn on BOTH sides of the diagonal.

mcqs.q: Parallelogram PQRS has PQ = 5.9 cm, QR = 4.1 cm and angle PQR = 65°. What is drawn first?
mcqs.why: First draw side PQ 5.9 cm long. Then make the 65° angle at Q with a protractor and mark QR = 4.1 cm on that ray.

mcqs.q: In the same parallelogram PQRS, how is the fourth corner S found?
options: By arcs of 4.1 cm from P and 5.9 cm from R
mcqs.why: Draw an arc from P equal to QR (4.1 cm) and an arc from R equal to PQ (5.9 cm) with a compass. Their crossing point is S, because opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal.

mcqs.q: Parallelogram ABCD has AB = 6.6 cm, AD = 4 cm and angle BAD = 50°. At which point is the 50° angle made?
mcqs.why: The 50° angle BAD is made at A with a protractor, after drawing AB = 6.6 cm. Side AD = 4 cm is then marked on that ray.

mcqs.q: Parallelogram CDEF has CD = 63 mm and DE = 39 mm. What is the length of the side opposite CD?
mcqs.why: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal, so the side opposite CD (63 mm) is also 63 mm. The side opposite DE is 39 mm.

mcqs.q: Parallelogram ABCD has BC = 6 cm, CD = 4 cm and diagonal BD = 7.3 cm. What is drawn first in this (Part B) method?
mcqs.why: In Part B the diagonal is drawn first: BD = 7.3 cm. Then arcs of 6 cm from B and 4 cm from D form triangle BCD, and the arcs are repeated on the other side to find A.

mcqs.q: Why can triangle BCD (sides 6 cm, 4 cm, diagonal 7.3 cm) be formed?
mcqs.why: The triangle inequality holds: 6 + 4 = 10 > 7.3 (and 7.3 + 4 > 6). Without this, the arcs would never meet and the parallelogram could not be built.

mcqs.q: Parallelogram BDFH has BD = 50 mm, BH = 30 mm and diagonal HD = 64 mm. Which segment is drawn first?
mcqs.why: The diagonal HD = 64 mm is drawn first. Arcs of 30 mm from H and 50 mm from D form triangle HDB; note 30 + 50 > 64, so it is possible.

mcqs.q: Parallelogram RSTU has RS = 59 mm, ST = 36 mm and diagonal TR = 7.5 cm. How long is TR in mm?
mcqs.why: TR = 7.5 cm = 75 mm. Units must be the same before constructing: 59 + 36 = 95 > 75, so the triangle on the diagonal can be formed.

mcqs.q: Parallelogram UVWX has UX = 7 cm, UV = 5 cm and diagonal VX = 9 cm. What check shows the construction is possible?
mcqs.why: Check: 5 + 7 = 12 > 9, so the two sides and the diagonal satisfy the triangle inequality. Draw diagonal VX first, then arcs of 5 cm and 7 cm on both sides.

mcqs.q: In Part B, after the first triangle is built on the diagonal, how is the parallelogram completed?
options: By drawing the same two arcs on the other side of the diagonal and joining that point
mcqs.why: The same two side-length arcs are drawn on the other side of the diagonal. Joining that second crossing point to both ends of the diagonal completes the parallelogram, since opposite sides are equal.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.6 — Checking Angle Sums
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

This is measuring work, not construction. You use a protractor to measure the angles of triangles and quadrilaterals, add them, and check two famous rules.

Formula / Rule

Sum of the three angles of any triangle = 180°

Sum of the four angles of any quadrilateral = 360°

Worked Example

Checking a triangle with angles 60°, 70° and 50°.

Step 1: Measure the first angle with a protractor: 60°.

Step 2: Measure the second angle: 70°.

Step 3: Measure the third angle: 50°.

Step 4: Add them: 60° + 70° + 50° = 180°. The rule is confirmed.

Remember

  • A right triangle example: 90° + 60° + 30° = 180°.
  • A square or rectangle example: 90° + 90° + 90° + 90° = 360°.
  • A parallelogram example: 70° + 110° + 70° + 110° = 360°.
  • The rule holds for every triangle and every quadrilateral, whatever its shape or type.

mcqs.q: What is the sum of the three angles of any triangle?
mcqs.why: The sum of the three angles of a triangle is always 180°. You check this by measuring all three angles with a protractor and adding them.

mcqs.q: A triangle has angles 60°, 70° and 50°. What is their sum?
mcqs.why: 60° + 70° + 50° = 180°. This is the book's example showing that the angle sum of a triangle is 180°.

mcqs.q: A right triangle has angles 90°, 60° and 30°. What is their sum?
mcqs.why: 90° + 60° + 30° = 180°. Even a right triangle, with one angle of exactly 90°, still has a total angle sum of 180°.

mcqs.q: What is the sum of the four angles of any quadrilateral?
mcqs.why: The sum of the four angles of a quadrilateral is always 360°. Measure the four angles with a protractor and add them to check.

mcqs.q: A quadrilateral has four angles of 90° each. What is their sum?
mcqs.why: 90° + 90° + 90° + 90° = 360°. This is the case of a square or rectangle, where every angle is a right angle.

mcqs.q: A parallelogram has angles 70°, 110°, 70° and 110°. What is their sum?
mcqs.why: 70° + 110° + 70° + 110° = 360°. Opposite angles of the parallelogram are equal, and all four together still make 360°.

mcqs.q: Which instrument is used to measure the angles in this exercise?
mcqs.why: A protractor measures angles in degrees. In Exercise 11.6 it is used on the given triangles (ABC, DEF, MNL, PQR) and quadrilaterals to verify the angle sums.

mcqs.q: How many triangles are given in Question I of this exercise to measure and check?
mcqs.why: Question I gives four triangles: ABC, DEF, MNL and PQR. For each one, the three measured angles must add up to 180°.

mcqs.q: How many quadrilaterals are given in Question III of this exercise?
options: Six (ABCD, PQRS, OLNM, CDEF, TWXY, MQOP)
mcqs.why: Question III gives six quadrilaterals: ABCD, PQRS, OLNM, CDEF, TWXY and MQOP. For each one, the four measured angles must add up to 360°.

mcqs.q: In Questions II and IV, what kinds of figures does the student draw and check?
options: Triangles and quadrilaterals of different types, e.g. right, acute, obtuse triangles and a rectangle and a parallelogram
mcqs.why: The student draws two or more triangles of different types (right, acute, obtuse) and two or more quadrilaterals (like a rectangle and a parallelogram). Whatever the type, the sums stay 180° and 360°.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 11 — Practical Geometry: Mixed Practice
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

This review covers the whole unit: definitions, angle sums, dividing segments, and constructing triangles and parallelograms.

A line segment is the part of a straight line with two end points; it has a fixed length and can be measured. Two line segments are congruent when their lengths are equal. A triangle is a closed figure of three sides with angle sum 180°. A quadrilateral is a closed figure of four sides with angle sum 360°; its types are square, rectangle, parallelogram, rhombus, trapezium and kite.

An altitude is the perpendicular distance from a vertex to the opposite side. The vertex angle is the angle between the two equal sides of an isosceles triangle. A square is at the same time a rectangle, a parallelogram and a rhombus.

Formula / Rule

Sum of angles of a triangle = 180°; sum of angles of a quadrilateral = 360°

Each angle of an equilateral triangle = 60°; vertex angle = 180° − 2 × Base angle

Construction Steps — Worked Example

Divide a 10.5 cm segment in the ratio 3 : 4.

Step 1: Draw a segment 10.5 cm long.

Step 2: Draw a ray at an acute angle from one end and mark 3 + 4 = 7 equal arcs with a compass.

Step 3: Join the seventh mark to the other end of the segment.

Step 4: Draw a parallel through the third mark to cut the segment.

Step 5: The parts are (3/7) × 10.5 = 4.5 cm and (4/7) × 10.5 = 6 cm.

Remember

  • Triangle types by sides: equilateral, isosceles, scalene. By angles: acute-angled, right-angled, obtuse-angled.
  • Equilateral triangle properties: all sides equal, all angles 60°, altitude bisects the base and the vertex angle.
  • An isosceles triangle with base angle 45° has vertex angle 90°; with vertex angle 56°, the base angle is (180° − 56°) ÷ 2 = 62°.

mcqs.q: The figure formed by joining three non-collinear points is called a:
mcqs.why: Joining three non-collinear points forms a triangle. A triangle is a simple closed figure with three sides, three vertices and three angles.

mcqs.q: What is a line segment?
options: A line with one end point
The part of a straight line which has two end points, a fixed length, and can be measured
A line with no end points
mcqs.why: A line segment is the part of a straight line which has two end points. Its properties are: it has a fixed length, it can be measured, and it has two end points.

mcqs.q: When are two line segments called congruent?
options: When they meet at a point
mcqs.why: Two line segments are congruent when their measures are equal. For example, if mOP = mQR, the segments OP and QR are equal in length.

mcqs.q: A quadrilateral whose four angles are right angles and whose opposite sides are equal is a:
mcqs.why: A rectangle has all four angles as right angles and opposite sides equal. A square also has right angles, but in a square all four sides are equal, not just the opposite ones.

mcqs.q: What is the sum of the four angles of a quadrilateral?
mcqs.why: The sum of the four angles of a quadrilateral is 360°. You can prove it by observation: measure the four angles of any quadrilateral with a protractor and add them.

mcqs.q: A quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel and equal is a:
mcqs.why: A parallelogram is defined by opposite sides being parallel and equal. Squares, rectangles and rhombuses are special parallelograms, but the plain name for this property is parallelogram.

mcqs.q: In an isosceles triangle the base angle is 45°. What is its vertex angle?
mcqs.why: Vertex angle = 180° − 2 × 45° = 180° − 90° = 90°. The vertex angle is the angle between the two equal sides of the triangle.

mcqs.q: Each angle of an equilateral triangle is:
mcqs.why: Each angle of an equilateral triangle is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°. All three sides are equal and all three angles are equal in an equilateral triangle.

mcqs.q: Is a square a rectangle, a parallelogram or a rhombus?
mcqs.why: A square is all three: a rectangle, a parallelogram and a rhombus. This is because all its angles are right angles, its opposite sides are parallel and equal, and all four sides are equal.

mcqs.q: An 11.9 cm segment is divided in the ratio 2 : 4 : 2. What is the middle part?
mcqs.why: Total parts = 2 + 4 + 2 = 8. The middle part = (4/8) × 11.9 = 5.95 cm, and the two end parts are each (2/8) × 11.9 = 2.975 cm. Parallels are drawn through the 2nd and 6th marks.

chapters.title: Circumference, Area and Volume of a Circle

lessons.title: Practical Work — Discovering π and the Area of a Circle
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

The distance around a circle is called its circumference. By measuring many circles we find a fixed number.

For every circle, circumference ÷ diameter is the same: about 3, exactly 22/7 ≈ 3.14. This number is called π (pi).

To measure the circumference of a cylinder, wrap a thread once around it, straighten the thread and measure it.

Cutting a circle into 16 sectors and arranging them makes a nearly rectangular shape. This gives the area formula.

Formula / Rule

Circumference = π × diameter

π = 22/7 ≈ 3.14

Area = πr²

Worked Example

Diameter = 3.5 cm, circumference = 11 cm. Find the ratio.

Step 1: Ratio = circumference ÷ diameter = 11 ÷ 3.5

Step 2: 11 ÷ 3.5 = 110/35 = 22/7 ≈ 3.14

Step 3: The same ratio comes from 88 ÷ 28, 13.2 ÷ 4.2 and 66 ÷ 21 — always 22/7.

For area: length of rectangle = π × radius, width = radius, so area = π × radius × radius = πr².

Remember

  • Circumference is about 3 times the diameter.
  • A thread measuring 44 cm around a cylinder means circumference = 44 cm.
  • The 16-sector arrangement has length = half the circumference = πr.

mcqs.q: The distance around a circle is called its:
mcqs.why: Practical Work Example 1 defines it: the distance around a circular disc is the circumference. It is about 3 times the diameter.

mcqs.q: Circumference ÷ diameter is always approximately:
mcqs.why: All measurements give the same ratio: 11÷3.5, 88÷28, 13.2÷4.2, 66÷21 all equal 22/7 ≈ 3.14. This constant is π.

mcqs.q: If diameter = 28 mm and circumference = 88 mm, the ratio is:
mcqs.why: Ratio = 88 ÷ 28 = 22/7 ≈ 3.14. This is table row (ii) of Practical Work. The ratio is the same for every circle.

mcqs.q: Circumference = ___ × diameter.
mcqs.why: Since circumference ÷ diameter = π, we get circumference = π × diameter. With diameter = 2r this also gives circumference = 2πr.

mcqs.q: To measure the circumference of a round box, the method uses:
options: A thread wrapped once around it
mcqs.why: Practical Work 12.1.2: mark a thread, wrap it once around the cylinder, straighten and measure between marks. That length is the circumference.

mcqs.q: If the thread around a cylinder measures 44 cm, the circumference is:
mcqs.why: The straightened thread length equals one full round of the cylinder. The example gives circumference = 44 cm directly.

mcqs.q: Cutting a circle into 16 sectors and arranging them gives a shape nearly like a:
mcqs.why: Practical Work 12.1.3 arranges 16 sectors into a nearly rectangular shape. Its length is πr and width is r, giving area = πr².

mcqs.q: In the sector rectangle, the length equals:
mcqs.why: Half the sectors face one way and half the other, so length = half the circumference = π × radius. Width = radius, so area = πr × r = πr².

mcqs.q: The area formula derived from sectors is:
mcqs.why: Area = length × width = (πr) × (r) = πr². This is how the area formula is derived in the practical work.

mcqs.q: Diameter = 4.2 cm, circumference = 13.2 cm. Ratio circumference ÷ diameter is:
mcqs.why: 13.2 ÷ 4.2 = 132/42 = 22/7 ≈ 3.14. Every row of the table gives this same ratio, which is π.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.1 — Circumference of a Circle
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

Circumference is the distance around a circle. We can find it from diameter or radius, and work backwards to find radius or diameter from circumference. The minute hand of a clock covers one circumference in one hour. Thread around a plate or tyre must be at least one circumference long. Use π = 22/7 in this exercise.

Formula / Rule

Circumference = π × diameter

Circumference = 2πr

Radius = circumference × 7 / 44

Diameter = circumference × 7 / 22

Worked Example

Find the circumference when diameter = 28 cm.

Step 1: Circumference = π × diameter

Step 2: = (22/7) × 28

Step 3: = 22 × 4 = 88 cm

From radius: radius 10.5 cm gives 2 × (22/7) × 10.5 = 66 cm. Backwards: circumference 88 cm gives radius = 88 × 7/44 = 14 cm.

Remember

  • Diameter 35 cm → 110 cm; 42 mm → 132 mm; 56 mm → 176 mm.
  • Radius 28 cm → 176 cm; radius 49 cm → 308 cm.
  • Plate diameter 21 cm needs 66 cm thread; table diameter 1.4 m needs 4.4 m thread.
  • Minute hand 1.4 cm covers 8.8 cm in one hour.

mcqs.q: Circumference of a circle with diameter 28 cm (π = 22/7) is:
mcqs.why: Circumference = π × diameter = (22/7) × 28 = 22 × 4 = 88 cm. This is Exercise 12.1 Part A Q1(1).

mcqs.q: Circumference with radius 10.5 cm is:
mcqs.why: Circumference = 2πr = 2 × (22/7) × 10.5 = 66 cm. Use 2πr when radius is given, πd when diameter is given.

mcqs.q: If circumference = 88 cm, the radius is:
mcqs.why: Radius = circumference × 7/44 = 88 × 7/44 = 14 cm. This is the reverse formula from Part C.

mcqs.q: If circumference = 44 cm, the diameter is:
