mcqs.why: Diameter = circumference × 7/22 = 44 × 7/22 = 14 cm. Diameter is twice the radius, and radius here would be 7 cm.

mcqs.q: Circumference with diameter 35 cm is:
mcqs.why: (22/7) × 35 = 22 × 5 = 110 cm. This is Part A Q1(2) in the book.

mcqs.q: Circumference with radius 49 cm is:
Minute hand length 1.4 cm covers in one hour:
mcqs.why: In one hour the tip makes one full round = circumference = 2 × (22/7) × 1.4 = 8.8 cm. This is Part E Q1(1).

mcqs.q: Thread needed around a plate of diameter 21 cm is:
mcqs.why: Minimum thread = circumference = (22/7) × 21 = 66 cm. This is Part F Q1(1) — one full wrap needs one circumference.

mcqs.q: If circumference = 176 cm, the radius is:
mcqs.why: Radius = 176 × 7/44 = 28 cm. Check: 2 × (22/7) × 28 = 176 cm, so the answer is correct.

mcqs.q: Circumference with radius 28 cm is:
mcqs.why: 2 × (22/7) × 28 = 2 × 22 × 4 = 176 cm. Diameter would be 56 cm, and (22/7) × 56 also gives 176 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.2 — Area of a Circle
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

Area is the surface covered by the circle, measured in square units (cm², mm², m²). We find area from radius or diameter, and work backwards to find radius or diameter from area. Use π = 22/7.

Formula / Rule

Area = πr²

Radius = √(area × 7 / 22)

Radius = diameter ÷ 2

Worked Example

Find the area when radius = 14 cm.

Step 1: Area = πr²

Step 2: = (22/7) × 14 × 14

Step 3: = 22 × 2 × 14 = 616 cm²

From diameter 21 cm: radius = 10.5 cm, area = (22/7) × 10.5 × 10.5 = 346.5 cm². Backwards: area 154 mm² gives radius = √(154 × 7/22) = √49 = 7 mm.

Remember

  • Radius 21 cm → area 1386 cm²; radius 35 mm → 3850 mm².
  • Area 2464 cm² → radius 28 cm; area 5544 mm² → radius 42 mm.
  • Always halve the diameter first before using πr².
  • If radius doubles, area becomes four times (πr² has r²).

mcqs.q: Area of a circle with radius 14 cm is:
mcqs.why: Area = πr² = (22/7) × 14 × 14 = 616 cm². This is Exercise 12.2 Part A Q1(1). Circumference would be 88 cm, not area.

mcqs.q: Area with radius 21 cm is:
mcqs.why: Area = (22/7) × 21 × 21 = 22 × 3 × 21 = 1386 cm². This is Part A Q1(3) in the book.

mcqs.q: If area = 154 mm², the radius is:
mcqs.why: Radius = √(area × 7/22) = √(154 × 7/22) = √49 = 7 mm. This reverse formula is used in Part B.

mcqs.q: Area with diameter 28 cm is:
mcqs.why: First radius = 28 ÷ 2 = 14 cm. Then area = (22/7) × 14 × 14 = 616 cm². Always halve diameter first (Part C).

mcqs.q: If area = 2464 cm², the radius is:
mcqs.why: Radius = √(2464 × 7/22) = √784 = 28 cm. Note 784 is r² before taking the square root.

mcqs.q: Area with radius 10.5 cm is:
mcqs.why: Area = (22/7) × 10.5 × 10.5 = 346.5 cm². This is Part A Q1(2); 66 cm would be the circumference.

mcqs.q: If area = 154 cm², the diameter is:
mcqs.why: Radius = √(154 × 7/22) = 7 cm, then diameter = 2 × 7 = 14 cm. Part D needs both steps: root first, then double.

mcqs.q: Area with diameter 8.4 cm is:
mcqs.why: Radius = 8.4 ÷ 2 = 4.2 cm. Area = (22/7) × 4.2 × 4.2 = 55.44 cm². This is Part C Q1(5).

mcqs.q: If area = 5544 mm², radius is:
mcqs.why: Radius = √(5544 × 7/22) = √1764 = 42 mm. The number under the root, 1764, is r², not r.

mcqs.q: Area with radius 35 mm is:
mcqs.why: Area = (22/7) × 35 × 35 = 22 × 5 × 35 = 3850 mm². This is Part A Q1(5) in the book.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.3 — Total Surface Area of a Cylinder
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

A cylinder has two circular ends and one curved surface. Total surface area counts all of them.

Curved surface area = 2πrh. Two ends = 2 × πr² = 2πr². Adding gives the total.

We also work backwards: find height from total area, or find radius and height when their sum and total area are given.

Formula / Rule

Total surface area = 2πr(r + h)

Curved surface area = 2πrh

h = total area ÷ (2πr) − r

Worked Example

Radius = 14 cm, height = 26 cm. Find total area.

Step 1: Total area = 2πr(r + h)

Step 2: = 2 × (22/7) × 14 × (14 + 26) = 88 × 40

Step 3: = 3520 cm²

Backwards: radius 10.5 cm, total area 1980 cm² gives h = 1980 ÷ 66 − 10.5 = 19.5 cm.

Remember

  • Radius 21 cm, height 29 cm → 6600 cm².
  • Radius 10 cm, height 18 cm → 1760 cm².
  • If r + h = 28 cm and total area = 1408 cm², then r = 8 cm and h = 20 cm.

mcqs.q: Total surface area of a cylinder is given by:
mcqs.why: Total area = curved surface 2πrh + two ends 2πr² = 2πr(r + h). The formula 2πrh alone is only the curved surface.

mcqs.q: Radius 14 cm, height 26 cm. Total area is:
Radius 21 cm, height 29 cm. Total area is:
Radius 10.5 cm, total area 1980 cm². Height is:
Radius 10 cm, height 18 cm. Total area is:
If r + h = 28 cm and total area = 1408 cm², radius is:
Curved surface area formula is:
mcqs.why: Curved surface (side only, without ends) = 2πrh. Total surface adds the two circular ends to this.

mcqs.q: Radius 17.5 mm, height 22.5 mm. Total area is:
Radius 28 cm, total area 10560 cm². Height is:
mcqs.why: h = 10560 ÷ 176 − 28 = 60 − 28 = 32 cm. 2πr here is 176. This is Part B Q1(5).

mcqs.q: If r + h = 35 cm and total area = 3300 cm², height is:
mcqs.why: r = 3300 ÷ 220 = 15 cm, so h = 35 − 15 = 20 cm. This is Part C Q1(2) in the book.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.4 — Volume of a Cylinder
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

Volume is the space inside a cylinder, measured in cubic units (cm³, m³). Volume = area of circular base × height.

We also work backwards: find height from volume and radius, or find radius from volume and height (needs a square root at the end).

Formula / Rule

Volume = πr²h

h = volume ÷ (πr²)

r² = volume ÷ (πh), then r = √r²

Worked Example

Radius = 14 cm, height = 20 cm. Find volume.

Step 1: Volume = πr²h

Step 2: = (22/7) × 14 × 14 × 20

Step 3: = 22 × 2 × 14 × 20 = 12320 cm³

Backwards: radius 14 cm, volume 15400 cm³ gives h = 15400 ÷ 616 = 25 cm. Height 20 m, volume 12320 m³ gives r² = 196, so r = 14 m.

Remember

  • Radius 28 cm, height 40 cm → 98560 cm³.
  • Diameter 70 mm means radius 35 mm first; volume with height 50 mm is 192500 mm³.
  • Volume uses r² — do not forget to square the radius.

mcqs.q: Volume of a cylinder is given by:
mcqs.why: Volume = base area × height = πr² × h = πr²h. The other formulas give surface areas or circumference, not volume.

mcqs.q: Radius 14 cm, height 20 cm. Volume is:
mcqs.why: (22/7) × 14 × 14 × 20 = 12320 cm³. This is Exercise 12.4 Part A Q1(1).

mcqs.q: Radius 28 cm, height 40 cm. Volume is:
Radius 14 cm, volume 15400 cm³. Height is:
Diameter 70 mm, height 50 mm. Volume is:
mcqs.why: First radius = 70 ÷ 2 = 35 mm. Volume = (22/7) × 35 × 35 × 50 = 192500 mm³. Halve diameter first (Part A Q7).

mcqs.q: Height 20 m, volume 12320 m³. Radius is:
mcqs.why: r² = 12320 ÷ ((22/7) × 20) = 196, so r = √196 = 14 m. Remember the final square-root step in Part C.

mcqs.q: Radius 20 cm, volume 35200 cm³. Height is:
Radius 20 cm, height 28 cm. Volume is:
mcqs.why: (22/7) × 20 × 20 × 28 = 35200 cm³. This is Part A Q1(4) in the book.

mcqs.q: Height 28 cm, volume 35200 cm³. Radius is:
mcqs.why: r² = 35200 ÷ 88 = 400, so r = √400 = 20 cm. 400 is r², not r — take the square root (Part C Q3).

mcqs.q: Radius 30 mm, volume 99000 mm³. Height is:

lessons.title: Exercise 12.5 — Circle Word Problems: Cost and Wire
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

Real-life problems use circumference for wire, fencing and distance, and area for grass, paving, polishing and cloth. Steps: find circumference or area first, then multiply by rounds or by cost per unit.

A wire bent from a square or triangle keeps the same length: perimeter of the old shape = circumference of the circle.

For a path between two circles: path area = outer area − inner area.

Formula / Rule

Circumference = 2πr = π × diameter

Area = πr²

Total cost = quantity × rate

Worked Example

Garden diameter 70 m, wire 5 times around, Rs. 10 per metre. Find cost.

Step 1: Circumference = (22/7) × 70 = 220 m

Step 2: 5 rounds = 5 × 220 = 1100 m

Step 3: Cost = 1100 × 10 = Rs. 11,000

Path example: outer radius 24.5 m, inner 17.5 m gives path area 1886.5 − 962.5 = 924 m², cost at Rs. 100 = Rs. 92,400.

Remember

  • Square side 22 cm bent to circle: perimeter 88 cm, radius 14 cm.
  • Wheel radius 42 cm in 1000 revolutions covers 2.64 km.
  • Field radius 14 m, grass at Rs. 20/m²: area 616 m², cost Rs. 12,320.

mcqs.q: Garden diameter 70 m, circumference is:
mcqs.why: Circumference = (22/7) × 70 = 220 m. For 5 rounds the wire is 1100 m and cost at Rs. 10/m is Rs. 11,000 (Q1).

mcqs.q: Wire of square side 22 cm is bent into a circle. Radius of circle is:
mcqs.why: Perimeter = 4 × 22 = 88 cm = circumference. Radius = 88 × 7/44 = 14 cm. Wire length stays the same (Q2).

mcqs.q: Bicycle wheel radius 42 cm covers in one revolution:
mcqs.why: One revolution = circumference = 2 × (22/7) × 42 = 264 cm = 2.64 m. In 1000 revolutions it covers 2.64 km (Q3).

mcqs.q: Wrapping 4 times cost Rs. 3960 at Rs. 5/m. Radius of field is:
mcqs.why: Wire length = 3960 ÷ 5 = 792 m. One round = 792 ÷ 4 = 198 m. Radius = 198 × 7/44 = 31.5 m (Q4).

mcqs.q: Equilateral triangle side 13.2 m bent into a circle. Diameter is:
mcqs.why: Perimeter = 3 × 13.2 = 39.6 m = circumference. Diameter = 39.6 × 7/22 = 12.6 m (Q5).

mcqs.q: Circular field radius 14 m. Area for grass is:
mcqs.why: Area = (22/7) × 14 × 14 = 616 m². At Rs. 20/m² the total cost is Rs. 12,320 (Q6).

mcqs.q: Outer diameter 49 m, inner 35 m. Path area is:
mcqs.why: Outer area 1886.5 m² minus inner area 962.5 m² gives path area 924 m². Paving at Rs. 100/m² costs Rs. 92,400 (Q7).

mcqs.q: Table diameter 2.8 m. Polishing area is:
mcqs.why: Radius = 1.4 m. Area = (22/7) × 1.4 × 1.4 = 6.16 m². At Rs. 100/m² cost is Rs. 616 (Q8).

mcqs.q: Fountain radius 3.5 m. Painting area is:
mcqs.why: Area = (22/7) × 3.5 × 3.5 = 38.5 m². At Rs. 75/m² total cost is Rs. 2,887.50 (Q9).

mcqs.q: Table cover diameter 3.5 m. Cloth area is:

lessons.title: Exercise 12.6 — Cylinder Word Problems: Tanks, Wells and Cost
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

Cylinder problems in daily life: cementing tanks, steel sheets, water capacity in litres, earth dug from wells, and tiling walls.

Open tank: steel/cement = bottom area + curved surface = πr² + 2πrh (no top).

Closed tank total: 2πr(r + h). Pipe open from both sides: only curved surface 2πrh.

Capacity: volume in cm³ ÷ 1000 = litres. Wall tiling uses curved surface only.

Formula / Rule

Curved surface = 2πrh

Total surface = 2πr(r + h)

Volume = πr²h

1 litre = 1000 cm³

Worked Example

Well diameter 7 m, depth 16 m. Volume of earth dug out?

Step 1: Radius = 7 ÷ 2 = 3.5 m

Step 2: Volume = (22/7) × 3.5 × 3.5 × 16

Step 3: = 616 m³

Tank example: radius 10.5 m, height 8 m, bottom + curved = 346.5 + 528 = 874.5 m², cost at Rs. 50 = Rs. 43,725.

Remember

  • Tank diameter 4.2 m, height 5 m holds 69,300 litres.
  • Mosque wall: radius 14 m, height 8.75 m, wall area 770 m², tiling cost Rs. 154,000 at Rs. 200/m².
  • Pool diameter 42 m, depth 5 m: wall area 660 m², cost Rs. 66,000 at Rs. 100/m².
  • Drum capacity 3850 litres with radius 0.7 m gives height 2.5 m.

mcqs.q: Tank radius 10.5 m, height 8 m. Bottom + curved area is:
mcqs.why: Bottom = 346.5 m², curved = 2 × (22/7) × 10.5 × 8 = 528 m². Total = 874.5 m². Cost at Rs. 50/m² is Rs. 43,725 (Q1).

mcqs.q: Steel tank radius 7 m, height 8.4 m. Total surface area is:
Open tank diameter 2.8 m, height 5 m. Steel needed is:
mcqs.why: Radius 1.4 m. Open tank = bottom 6.16 + curved 44 = 50.16 m² (no top). Cost at Rs. 300/m² is Rs. 15,048 (Q3).

mcqs.q: Pipe open from both sides uses which area?
mcqs.why: A pipe open from both sides has no ends, so only the curved surface 2πrh counts. Q4 gives 123.2 m² with the printed numbers.

mcqs.q: Tank diameter 4.2 m, height 5 m holds how many litres?
mcqs.why: Radius 210 cm, height 500 cm. Volume = 69,300,000 cm³. Divide by 1000 gives 69,300 litres (Q6).

mcqs.q: Well diameter 7 m, depth 16 m. Earth dug out is:
mcqs.why: Radius 3.5 m. Volume = (22/7) × 3.5 × 3.5 × 16 = 616 m³. The dug earth volume equals the well volume (Q8).

mcqs.q: Soft-drink can radius 3.5 cm, length 10.5 cm. Capacity is:
Well diameter 3.5 m, depth 24 m. Digging volume is:
Mosque diameter 28 m, wall height 8.75 m. Wall area is:
mcqs.why: Wall = curved surface = 2 × (22/7) × 14 × 8.75 = 770 m². Tiling at Rs. 200/m² costs Rs. 154,000 (Q13).

mcqs.q: Pool diameter 42 m, depth 5 m. Wall area is:
mcqs.why: Radius 21 m. Wall = 2 × (22/7) × 21 × 5 = 660 m². Cost at Rs. 100/m² is Rs. 66,000 (Q14).

lessons.title: Review Exercise 12 — Circle and Cylinder: Mixed Practice
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

Review of all Unit 12 formulas. Circumference is the distance around a circle. The ratio circumference ÷ diameter is always π = 22/7 ≈ 3.14.

Diameter is the chord through the centre; diameter = 2 × radius. A closed circular shape with two circular ends is a cylinder.

Formula / Rule

Circumference = π × diameter = 2πr

Area = πr²

Curved surface = 2πrh

Total surface = 2πr(r + h)

Volume = πr²h

Worked Example

Minute hand 3.5 cm long. Distance covered by tip in one hour?

Step 1: Distance = circumference = 2πr

Step 2: = 2 × (22/7) × 3.5

Step 3: = 22 cm

Also: diameter 7 cm gives circumference 22 cm; radius 1 cm gives area 22/7 cm² and cylinder volume (r=1, h=1) 22/7 cm³. If r = h, volume = πr³.

Remember

  • Value of π to two decimal places is 3.14; as a fraction 22/7.
  • If radius doubles, area becomes four times.
  • Two circular ends of a cylinder with r = 1 cm have total area 44/7 cm².
  • Total surface with r = 1 cm, h = 1 cm is 4π cm².

mcqs.q: The distance around a circle is called:
mcqs.why: Review Part A Q1: the distance around a circle is its circumference. Formula: circumference = π × diameter = 2πr.

mcqs.q: Circumference ÷ diameter always equals:
mcqs.why: Review Part A Q2: this ratio is constant for every circle and equals π. Its value is 22/7, about 3.14 to two decimal places.

mcqs.q: Relation between diameter and radius is:
mcqs.why: Review Part A Q3: diameter = 2 × radius, so radius = diameter ÷ 2. The diameter is the chord through the centre.

mcqs.q: Area of a circle from radius is:
mcqs.why: Review Part A Q4: area = πr². For radius 1 cm, area = 22/7 cm², as in Part C Q2.

mcqs.q: Total surface area of a cylinder is:
mcqs.why: Review Part A Q5: total = 2πr(r + h), which includes curved surface 2πrh plus the two ends 2πr².

mcqs.q: Volume of a cylinder is:
mcqs.why: Review Part A Q6: volume = base area × height = πr²h. For r = 1, h = 1, volume = 22/7.

mcqs.q: Circumference when diameter is 7 cm is:
mcqs.why: Circumference = (22/7) × 7 = 22 cm. This is Review Part C Q1, correct option (iv) 22.

mcqs.q: Minute hand 3.5 cm covers in one hour:
mcqs.why: Distance = 2 × (22/7) × 3.5 = 22 cm. One hour is one full round of the tip (Part C Q9).

mcqs.q: If radius of a circle is doubled, its area becomes:
mcqs.why: Area = πr². New area = π(2r)² = 4πr², i.e. four times. This is Part C Q10, because radius is squared.

mcqs.q: If radius and height of a cylinder are equal (r = h), volume becomes:
mcqs.why: Review Part A Q8: volume = πr²h, and with h = r it becomes πr² × r = πr³ (or πh³).

lessons.title: Exercise 13.1 — Frequency Tables and Class Intervals
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

Data is collected information, like marks or bills. To understand data we organise it into a frequency distribution table. We use tally marks to count, and the count for each group is its frequency. When there are many values, we group them into class intervals like 10–17, 18–25. The total of all frequencies equals the total number of observations.

Formula / Rule

Range = Maximum value − Minimum value

Class width = Range ÷ Number of class intervals

Total frequency = sum of all frequencies = total number of observations

Worked Example

Example: Marks of 30 students: maximum 50, minimum 10. Make 5 class intervals of equal width.

Step 1: Range = 50 − 10 = 40.

Step 2: Class width = 40 ÷ 5 = 8.

Step 3: Make intervals: 10–17, 18–25, 26–33, 34–41, 42–50.

Step 4: Count with tally marks: frequencies are 6, 5, 4, 6, 9.

Step 5: Check: 6 + 5 + 4 + 6 + 9 = 30 = total students. ✓

Remember

  • Books sold in a week: 24 + 25 + 27 + 28 + 22 + 30 + 21 = 177 books; each day has frequency 1 and total frequency is 7.
  • Electricity bills: max 7180, min 3560, range 3620, width for 5 classes ≈ 725; frequencies 2, 1, 3, 2, 4 total 12.
  • Zoo visitors (30 values): the busiest interval is 130–139 with frequency 6.
  • Some intervals can be empty, frequency 0 — still write them in the table.

mcqs.q: Books sold: Mon 24, Tue 25, Wed 27, Thu 28, Fri 22, Sat 30, Sun 21. Total books sold in the week is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 177. Add step by step: 24 + 25 + 27 + 28 + 22 + 30 + 21 = 177. In the frequency table each day has frequency 1, so total frequency is 7 days.

mcqs.q: Electricity bills: maximum 7180, minimum 3560. The range is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 3620. Range = maximum − minimum = 7180 − 3560 = 3620. Range shows how spread out the data is and is the first step before making classes.

mcqs.q: For the same bills, with 5 class intervals, the class width is about:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 724 ≈ 725. Class width = range ÷ number of classes = 3620 ÷ 5 = 724, rounded to 725 in the book. The five intervals then cover all 12 bills with frequencies 2, 1, 3, 2, 4.

mcqs.q: Marks of 30 students: maximum 50, minimum 10, 5 classes. The class width is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 8. Range = 50 − 10 = 40, and 40 ÷ 5 = 8. So the intervals are 10–17, 18–25, 26–33, 34–41 and 42–50.

mcqs.q: For the same marks, the interval 42–50 has frequency:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 9. Counting the marks from 42 to 50 with tally marks gives 9 students, the highest frequency in the table. The frequencies 6, 5, 4, 6, 9 add up to 30.

mcqs.q: Zoo visitors data has 30 values. Its total frequency must be:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 30. Total frequency always equals the total number of observations, here 30 visitor counts. If your frequencies do not add to 30, a counting mistake has been made.

mcqs.q: In the zoo table, the interval with the highest frequency 6 is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 130–139, with frequency 6. Six of the daily visitor numbers fall between 130 and 139. The next highest is 160–169 with frequency 5.

mcqs.q: In the zoo table, the interval 190–199 has frequency:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 0. No visitor number falls between 190 and 199, so the interval is empty but is still written in the table. Empty intervals are a normal part of a frequency table.

mcqs.q: In the marks out of 850 table with width 100, the interval 651–750 has frequency:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 9. With width 100 the 20 marks fall into 551–650 (6), 651–750 (9) and 751–850 (5). A bigger width gives fewer intervals; 6 + 9 + 5 = 20 checks the total.

mcqs.q: The number of observations falling in one category is called its:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is frequency. We count observations with tally marks and write the count as the frequency. This word is used in every frequency distribution table.

lessons.title: Exercise 13.2 — Pie Graphs: Finding Angles and Numbers
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

A pie graph shows data as slices (sectors) of a circle. The whole circle is 360° and stands for the total. A bigger share gets a bigger angle. To draw a pie graph, first find the angle for each part, check that the angles add to 360°, then draw the sectors with a protractor.

Formula / Rule

Angle of a part = (number in the part ÷ total) × 360°

Number from an angle = (angle ÷ 360°) × total

Sum of all sector angles = 360°

Worked Example

Example: 80 students, 60 passed and 20 failed. Find the pie graph angles.

Step 1: Total = 80.

Step 2: Pass angle = (60 ÷ 80) × 360° = 270°.

Step 3: Fail angle = (20 ÷ 80) × 360° = 90°.

Step 4: Check: 270° + 90° = 360°. ✓

Step 5: Draw a circle and make sectors of 270° and 90°.

Remember

  • Half of the total gives 180°, one quarter gives 90°, three quarters gives 270°.
  • Colours in a class of 36: red 160°, blue 90°, pink 70°, white 40°.
  • Fruits (total 60): banana has the biggest sector, 144°, because 24 is the largest number.
  • Always check: all angles together must make exactly 360°.

mcqs.q: 80 students, 60 passed. The angle for Pass in the pie graph is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 270°. Angle = (60 ÷ 80) × 360° = 270°, which is three quarters of the circle. The Fail angle is the remaining 90°, and 270° + 90° = 360°.

mcqs.q: For the same class, the angle for Fail (20 students) is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 90°. Angle = (20 ÷ 80) × 360° = 90°, exactly one quarter of the circle. A quick check is 360° − 270° = 90°.

mcqs.q: 36 students like colours: 16 red, 9 blue, 7 pink, 4 white. The angle for blue is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 90°. Angle = (9 ÷ 36) × 360° = 90°. Red is 160°, pink is 70° and white is 40°, and all four add to 360°.

mcqs.q: For the same colours, the angle for red (16 students) is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 160°. Angle = (16 ÷ 36) × 360° = 160°, the largest sector because red has the most students. In a pie graph the largest number always gets the largest angle.

mcqs.q: Fruit shop: 12 apples, 24 bananas, 16 mangoes, 8 peaches (total 60). The angle for bananas is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 144°. Angle = (24 ÷ 60) × 360° = 144°. Apples are 72°, mangoes 96° and peaches 48°, totalling 360°.

mcqs.q: For the same fruits, the angle for peaches (8) is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 48°. Angle = (8 ÷ 60) × 360° = 48°, the smallest sector because peaches are the fewest. Smallest number means smallest angle in a pie graph.

mcqs.q: Party food total is 720: 180 cold drinks, 124 sandwiches, 330 burgers, 86 samosas. The angle for cold drinks is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 90°. Angle = (180 ÷ 720) × 360° = 90°, since 180 is one quarter of 720. Burgers get 165°, sandwiches 62° and samosas 43°.

mcqs.q: For the same party, the angle for burgers (330) is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 165°. Angle = (330 ÷ 720) × 360° = 165°, the biggest sector because burgers are the most in number. The four angles 90° + 62° + 165° + 43° = 360°.

mcqs.q: A pie graph shows favourite foods of 180 students: chicken 180°. How many students like chicken?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 90 students. Number = (angle ÷ 360°) × total = (180 ÷ 360) × 180 = 90. Half the circle means half the students.

mcqs.q: In the same graph, noodles have angle 50°. How many students like noodles?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 25 students. Number = (50 ÷ 360) × 180 = 25. In the same way pachiyon at 40° gives 20 students, the least favourite food.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 13 — Data Handling: Mixed Practice
lessons.notes_html:
The Main Idea

This review covers the key words of data handling and one full frequency table. Learn the meanings first: data, frequency, tally marks, lower limit, upper limit, class width and pie graph. Then practise making a table: find the minimum, make intervals of the given width, count with tally marks, and check that the frequencies add up to the total number of observations.

Formula / Rule

Range = Maximum − Minimum; Class width = Range ÷ Number of intervals

Class width of one interval = Upper limit − Lower limit (as used in this book's intervals)

Sum of angles in a pie graph = 360°

Worked Example

Example: Maximum 21, minimum 3, make 3 class intervals. Find the class width. Also do the park ages table check.

Step 1: Range = 21 − 3 = 18.

Step 2: Class width = 18 ÷ 3 = 6.

Step 3: For the park ages, minimum is 1 and width is 10, so intervals are 1–10, 11–20, 21–30, 31–40, 41–50.

Step 4: Frequencies are 7, 11, 10, 9, 3.

Step 5: Check: 7 + 11 + 10 + 9 + 3 = 40 visitors. ✓

Remember

  • Collected information is called data; dividing data into class intervals is called organising the data.
  • The smaller number of a class interval is its lower limit; the larger number is its upper limit.
  • The marks put against each observation are tally marks.
  • A graph that shows data in the form of a circle is a pie graph.

mcqs.q: Collected information is called:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is data. Data is the raw collected information, like marks or ages, before it is organised. We then organise data into tables and graphs.

mcqs.q: The number of observations falling in one category is called:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the frequency. For example, in the park table the interval 11–20 has frequency 11. Frequencies are counted using tally marks.

mcqs.q: The marks put against each observation are called:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is tally marks. We put one tally mark for each observation in its interval, then count the marks to get the frequency. Tally marks make counting large data safe and easy.

mcqs.q: The smaller number of a class interval is called the:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the lower limit. In the interval 9–12, the lower limit is 9 and the upper limit is 12. Lower means the smaller end of the interval.

mcqs.q: In the class interval 10–50, the upper limit is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 50. The upper limit is the larger number of the interval, here 50, while 10 is the lower limit. Always read the second number for the upper limit in this book's intervals.

mcqs.q: Dividing data into class intervals is called ______ the data.
mcqs.why: The correct answer is organising. Grouping values into class intervals like 1–10 and 11–20 organises the data so it can be read easily. A table made this way is a frequency table.

mcqs.q: The graph in which data is shown in the form of a circle is called a:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a pie graph. Its sectors are parts of a full circle of 360°, and each sector's angle is (part ÷ total) × 360°. The whole circle stands for the whole total.

mcqs.q: The sum of the angles of all sectors in a pie graph is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 360°. A full circle has 360°, so all sector angles together must make 360°. Use this as a check after finding every angle.

mcqs.q: Maximum 21, minimum 3, 3 class intervals. The class width is:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 6. Range = 21 − 3 = 18, and class width = 18 ÷ 3 = 6. First find the range, then divide by the number of intervals.

mcqs.q: Park visitors (40 ages), width 10, intervals from 1. The interval 11–20 has frequency:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 11. Counting the ages from 11 to 20 with tally marks gives 11 visitors, the highest frequency. The full table is 7, 11, 10, 9, 3, which adds to 40.
